sources.title: How Jack Friks grows apps with organic Instagram/TikTok posts and zero ad spend
sources.originalTitle: I Built a $670/Day SaaS App with NO Paid Ads
sources.summary: Jack Friks explains his organic social playbook for driving app downloads for free: new niche-only accounts, a week of warm-up, one post a day, copying proven formats, and iterating until something hits. He stresses relevance to the product and clear calls to action over raw views.

principles.text: Make a fresh account per business and only scroll your niche so the algorithm knows who to push you to.
principles.quote: I make a new account for whatever business I'm in. That's the first step to doing this. You make a new account because it's just easier this way.

principles.text: Find content ideas by saving already-viral videos in your niche, and bring formats over from other niches.
principles.quote: you're going to find a ton of content that's already viral for your target audience if you're scrolling and only engaging with your niche and then you just save it for later.

principles.text: Warm up a new account for about a week and post manually, one per day, so it isn't treated like a bot.
principles.quote: for the first week, I would not post any videos. And when you do post your first video, only post like one a day.

principles.text: Optimize for relevance and conversion, not max views: include a clear call to action and don't make it look like an ad.
principles.quote: you don't want to just make content for max views. You want to make content that's highly relevant to what you're promoting.

principles.text: Expect many iterations; change an angle each time rather than repeating the same video.
principles.quote: Usually people end up having to post 30 videos before they see something like do well.

principles.text: Do it manually first before automating; develop taste through around 100 pieces of content.
principles.quote: if you can't do it manually, there's no point of automating it because you're not going to know what works and what doesn't.

sources.title: How Jack Friks built four apps by scrolling TikTok daily and copying proven viral formats
sources.originalTitle: He Went From Struggling to Make $1 From His App to Turning Down $1M
sources.summary: Jack Friks explains how he went from eight months of near-zero revenue to a $15k month and a 100k-download app by scrolling his niche daily and copying formats that already work. He also covers building on proven niches, testing paywalls, staying solo and profitable, and turning down a $1M offer because he enjoyed the work.

principles.text: Be a daily user of the platform you market on; you can't learn what works by only posting.
principles.quote: you're not going to figure it out just posting and not being on the platform. You have to be a user.

principles.text: Copy what's already working in a viral format instead of inventing from scratch, then reuse it relentlessly.
principles.quote: if you can try to get some of what's working for an existing viral video rather than starting over from scratch, I think that's the best way to go.

principles.text: Once a format hits, keep reusing it; making something new costs far more effort than repeating a proven format. But expect it to run dry.
principles.quote: it takes way more effort to make something new than something that you know that works.

principles.text: Make organic content that doesn't look like an ad, and put the call to action in a pinned comment or caption.
principles.quote: all the videos I try to make they try to make them look not like ads.

principles.text: Build apps in niches where a successful counterpart already exists, and borrow its marketing.
principles.quote: everything I've made, not only a personal like I guess solution, but like a revamp of something that is already extremely working and successful and making money.

principles.text: Stay solo and small, optimize for profitability and fun, and don't sell just because the offer is big.
principles.quote: profitability is like the number one metric to be able to keep going

sources.title: How Jack Friks got 100k+ app downloads with zero ads using organic short-form media
sources.originalTitle: How to Get 100,000 Downloads with Zero Ads
sources.summary: Jack Friks explains how he drove 100,000+ free downloads to his mobile app by posting non-salesy short-form content on Instagram and TikTok, with the call to action only in the caption and pinned comment. He also covers validating ideas through organic media before building, and how this led him to build Post Bridge to schedule and template content at scale.

principles.text: Don't make the content an ad. Keep the video related to your niche and put the call to action only in the caption and pinned comment.
principles.quote: if you make it an ad and you're doing organic you're going to get like you're going to get a 100 200 views every single time the less call to action you have even if you have none you're going to perform better on the views

principles.text: Find formats by scrolling your niche: save posts that went viral, ask why they worked, and replicate the replicable ones as templates.
principles.quote: I just find things that have went viral and I kind of think about why like what drove these comments why did people like the video why did they watch the whole thing is this can this be replicated into a format

principles.text: Distribution is a volume game: output is limited by how many videos you can make and how many warmed-up accounts you have.
principles.quote: the limit is how much videos are you able to create and how many accounts you have that are warmed up that you can post to and like that's the only real factors that I think stop anyone from like scaling further

principles.text: Validate demand with organic content before building: if a pain point can't go viral organically, it's probably not a good business.
principles.quote: if you can't get a a Content format to go viral that has a a problem with your product as the solution then it's probably not a good business to build

principles.text: Build tools that solve your own problem; that's how his apps and Post Bridge came about, and it gave a high hit rate.
principles.quote: the main two ideas I had both worked out pretty well like the batting average of like idea to actually making money has been really high just following that like simple curve of like just building what I need for myself

principles.text: Post the same media to every channel, but optimize for the one where your audience is and where you scroll; extra channels are free reach.
principles.quote: I Target Instagram optimize for Instagram I scroll on Instagram if I'm going to find formats and then I just post a Tik Tok for like just extra views whatever extra reach happens

sources.title: Jack Friks: Building PostBridge by scratching your own itch and staying human on social media
sources.originalTitle: 396: Jack Friks - Building Tools That Empower Without Overwhelming
sources.summary: Jack explains how he built PostBridge, a simple social scheduler, because existing tools were too expensive and bloated for posting short videos for his app. He covers building in public without chasing followers, staying kind, keeping a product lean, and avoiding AI for content to keep an authentic voice.

principles.text: Build the tool for yourself first; a product you use daily stays simple and valuable, and you don't have to compete on small features.
principles.quote: I focused on building it for myself. ... I made it like as simple as possible and as useful as possible for me, which turned out to be very useful for other people.

principles.text: Compete with a fair price and real value, not comparisons. Point people to pricing and features and let word of mouth do the work.
principles.quote: my angle was just to make something that really gives people a valuable like something of value for a very fair price. And I don't have to like say, "Oh, this is better, that's better, this is better."

principles.text: Do the work, then document it. Followers are a byproduct of doing something interesting, not the goal.
principles.quote: I post, I do something, and it grows my business, and then as a byproduct, it grows my followers, which is kind of like the opposite of how some people are maybe approaching it

principles.text: Being human with flaws and raw thoughts stands out in a feed full of non-human content.
principles.quote: if you're honest, if you're being yourself, if you're being a human, it's going to stand out.

principles.text: Keep the product lean by filtering every feature through simplicity; add only what doesn't complicate the first-time user's workflow.
principles.quote: I'm constantly thinking everything I do, is this something that is going to bloat the software and make it less valuable to like a normal firsttime user?

principles.text: Keep using a content format that works until results actually stop, instead of switching out of boredom; iterate when it dies.
principles.quote: usually people switch it out before the results stop drying up, which is weird. ... if you have something that works, you keep using it.

sources.title: How Jack Friks found a working TikTok format and hit $3.2k MRR in week 6 of a couples app
sources.originalTitle: making a $10k/month app in 2 months (week 6 update)
sources.summary: Jack updates his 2-month push to build a $10k/month consumer app. A daily burner-phone TikTok routine found a replicable video format that drove 11,000 downloads in 48 hours. He then moved the app to freemium and plans to reinvest into UGC creator accounts to scale the format.

principles.text: Don't invent a format: scroll a fresh account, find videos in your niche that already performed, and recreate them.
principles.quote: You're not trying to recreate the wheel here.

principles.text: Native-feeling videos that show a cool feature beat ads; people forgive the app being visible if the feature is something they want.
principles.quote: it's showcasing a really cool feature that they want. So that's enough to get over that hill of appearing as an ad.

principles.text: Optimize for downloads, not views: judge formats by conversion to installs, since views can be misleading.
principles.quote: this one gets 100k views and brings in a th000 downloads so this format is clearly much better

principles.text: Reach your exact audience: target the people who'd use the product together, here couples downloading a couples app.
principles.quote: that's really the goal is to get couples to download the couples app.

principles.text: Seed deliberate small errors to trigger comments; the algorithm rewards comment activity.
principles.quote: The algorithm loves when people comment. If they're commenting, they're watching the video.

principles.text: Once a format works, milk it with repetition and scale it across many accounts using UGC creators, accepting it will eventually wear out.
principles.quote: Eventually it won't work so effectively. It will be overused but for now um basically going to milk it.

sources.title: How Jack Friks built and launched a couples mobile app in 5 days and got its first revenue
sources.originalTitle: how i went from idea to $$$ in 5 days (mobile app)
sources.summary: Jack built a Swift couples app in about 3 days using Claude Code in Cursor with no hand-written code, and launched it with a build-in-public tweet that drew half a million views. He explains his plan to scale it: find a short-form content format that converts, then automate posting.

principles.text: Build in public and tweet results; sharing what you build can drive early downloads even outside your target audience.
principles.quote: that is by me tweeting about it because I do tweet about what I build. A lot of people are interested in that.

principles.text: AI coding tools let you ship a mobile app without writing code; you give direction, tweak and fix bugs.
principles.quote: I didn't touch a single line of code. And I did double check all the security rules for Firebase.

principles.text: Grow a consumer app by finding a content format that works, then repeating it over and over.
principles.quote: this is a format that worked that I repeated over and over again once I found that it worked and it brought in downloads.

principles.text: Direct ads feel like ads and don't connect; test content formats until one converts to paying downloads.
principles.quote: I am testing out content formats and that is what brings me to how I'm going to scale this, which is once I find a content format.

principles.text: Once content performs manually, automate posting to scale rather than posting by hand.
principles.quote: Once my content is performing good, posting manually, scale it using PostBridge.

principles.text: Formats get milked dry, so keep iterating on a working format instead of relying on it forever.
principles.quote: it doesn't work as well anymore um because I haven't iterated on it. It's kind of been milked dry

sources.title: How Jack Friks took a new mobile app to ~$6k in 4 weeks, and his plan to reach $10k/month
sources.originalTitle: building a $10k/month mobile app in 2 months (week 4 update)
sources.summary: Week-4 update on a couples app: a viral Twitter post drove about 30,000 downloads overnight and roughly $6k in proceeds, with $2,800 MRR. Jack admits the luck, then lays out a repeatable plan: copy proven short-video formats, double down on hits, automate posting, and make the app free to try for better ratings and word of mouth.

principles.text: Viral luck is not repeatable, so build a repeatable organic content system instead.
principles.quote: I don't think that this is going to happen again. A random huge uh viral post on Twitter. So, I'm planning on now um using uh social media

principles.text: Copy proven content formats and apply them to your own app; entertaining stories beat plain promotion.
principles.quote: you have to make content that is good, that is entertaining, that tells a story, and that is using a proven format that other pieces of content have used, but then applying it to your own app.

principles.text: When a piece of content hits, recreate it in different ways and double down, then automate.
principles.quote: once one of them hits like 10,000 plus views, double down on it, make it again in a different way, and then once I have that ball rolling, use PostBridge

principles.text: Document the build publicly on Twitter; it works as a marketing channel.
principles.quote: Twitter can actually be a great marketing channel. I've been using it to document everything going on with this app.

principles.text: Let people use the app before paying so ratings improve and word of mouth can spread.
principles.quote: now that it's premium, if you know, someone wants to share with their friend, they can. And their friend can use it without putting up their credit card

principles.text: The core goal is a good app people want to use and eventually pay for.
principles.quote: it's a good app and that is the main goal here is to make a good app that people want to use and eventually pay for.

sources.title: Building a viral mobile app in 30 days, Day 1: solve your own problem and scope two core features
sources.originalTitle: building a viral mobile app in 30 days - day 1: idea and core features
sources.summary: Jack Friks kicks off a 30-day mobile app challenge by scoping "Doof", a junk-food diary with a coin-flip feature, built around his own problem. He walks through his idea-scoping doc, hard paywall and local-data decisions, an Expo plus Superwall boilerplate, vibe coding in Cursor, and why marketing is most of the work.

principles.text: Build something that solves your own problem; it's the easiest way to make what users want.
principles.quote: the most important thing is just that you're solving your own problem so that's what my idea is about

principles.text: Scope the idea first: define the problem, how it solves it, and one to three core features, with bonus features parked.
principles.quote: you have an idea that's fleshed out you have things defined and you know how it's going to solve a specific problem in one to three core features

principles.text: Ideas are worth little; execution matters, and the idea only multiplies how well you execute.
principles.quote: ideas are worth very little it's all about the execution like the idea is only a multiplier for how good you execute

principles.text: Marketing is most of the work; a great app without marketing gets no downloads or money.
principles.quote: the marketing is like 75% of the work you can make an amazing app but if you don't have good marketing you're not going to get downloads

principles.text: Use a hard paywall with a 7-day free trial; it converts much better than freemium.
principles.quote: a 7-Day free trial with a hard pay wall tends to convert much much better in into sales into money

principles.text: Ship the app fast so there's time for store review and for warming up social accounts, which can take a week alone.
principles.quote: we want to get the app out as soon as possible within the first two weeks because we're going to have to go through review and we're going to have to start warming up social media accounts

sources.title: How Jack Friks lost $500,000 in crypto income: tax mistakes and choosing work you want to do
sources.originalTitle: How I lost $500,000 last year at 22 years old.
sources.summary: Jack recounts earning about $500K from a crypto YouTube channel, an NFT sellout and mining, then losing most of it to crypto-denominated tax bills, developer costs and poor accounting decisions. He closes by pivoting to a topic he wants to work on long term, valuing what he does over how much he makes.

principles.text: Know your tax liability before you hold crypto income; taxes are owed at the price received, not at the later price.
principles.quote: all of the income that I made was paid in cryptocurrency so my income tax is based around the price that I received it at not whatever price it is when taxes roll around

principles.text: Serving a niche no one else is serving gives you a real opening to grow quickly.
principles.quote: basically I'm in a niche that no one is serving and I am here to now serve it

principles.text: Build toward owning something you can sell to your audience so you control your time and income.
principles.quote: one video per day and make something I can sell to my audience so I can control my own time and my own income on the internet

principles.text: Paying people does not equal progress; unmanaged spend on contractors burns money fast.
principles.quote: I was paying people to do things that didn't actually make any progress and my accountant even dropped me

principles.text: Don't chase easy money; pick work you'd actually want to do for the rest of your life.
principles.quote: easy money will elude you just like it did me so don't go for easy go for doing something you actually want to do for the rest of your life

principles.text: What you do day to day matters more than how much money you make or lose.
principles.quote: what you're doing matters a lot not how much money you're making or have lost

sources.title: Why $50/day online keeps Jack Friks happily unemployed: autonomy and scalable leverage
sources.originalTitle: making $50/day online keeps me happily unemployed
sources.summary: Jack reflects on hitting about $50/day from an app with premium features, and why that small number buys autonomy and keeps him out of a job. He argues for owning a scalable product, helping people genuinely, and treating paying users as real validation.

principles.text: Aim for autonomy, not just income: a small online income can keep a job away and fund time freedom.
principles.quote: if you want you can escape that cycle of the job okay you don't have to I'm not saying everyone should I'm just saying if you you could

principles.text: Prefer owning scalable leverage: a built product makes $50 and $500 a day with about the same effort.
principles.quote: for me to make $50 a day versus me to make 500 it's about the same amount of effort

principles.text: A built product doesn't have to be rebuilt per sale, so marginal cost is tiny and revenue can scale.
principles.quote: I've already made the app people are paying for the to use the apps uh premium features or take away ads whatever may be and I don't have to make that again every time when someone buys the thing so it's scalable

principles.text: Profit only comes from genuinely helping people; aim to over-deliver on value.
principles.quote: that's the only way to do anything really um that makes profits or makes a money is to actually help people otherwise you're running a fugazi

principles.text: Paying customers are far stronger validation than kind comments and keep you going.
principles.quote: people paying me for my product that maybe this actually could work and actually it can because people are paying me for it and they're telling me they like it which is IM immensely more valuable than people just commenting

principles.text: Owning the business means you capture the full upside and see direct cause and effect.
principles.quote: any awards you make are going to come back right to you which is really good if I make $10,000 because it had a really good day or something well guess what I don't just get paid a bonus I get paid the $10,000

sources.title: How Jack Friks took Curiosity Quench from a no-code web app to $30K in 365 days
sources.originalTitle: day 365 of making an app to END DOOMSCROLLING (1 year progress update!)
sources.summary: A one-year progress update on building Curiosity Quench, an app that replaces doomscrolling with activities matched to people's curiosity. Jack walks through the timeline from a no-code web prototype and viral clips to 95K downloads and $30K revenue, with half of that revenue landing in the last two months.

principles.text: Document the build publicly before you have anything to show; talking about the idea can attract feedback and early demand.
principles.quote: لم أفعل شيئاً حقاً أو يكن لدي أي شيء لأعرضه في الشهر الأول. كنت أتحدث فقط عن الفكرة ويبدو أن الكثير من الناس أحبوها.

principles.text: Start with a crude no-code version instead of waiting until you can code it properly.
principles.quote: لم يكن تطبيقاً للهواتف المحمولة في الأشهر الأربعة الأولى. كان تطبيقاً للويب. لقد صنعت نسخة بدون برمجة.

principles.text: When results are low for months, look for real signs of interest and keep going rather than quitting.
principles.quote: إذا كان هناك 300 ألف مشاهدة حقيقية لي وأنا أعرض تطبيق ويب رديء جداً، فأنا متأكد من وجود اهتمام.

principles.text: Daily consistency compounds; a year passes fast if you commit every day.
principles.quote: ثقوا بي، يمر الوقت بسرعة إذا التزمت كل يوم.

principles.text: Past a point, marketing matters more than product polish, since people can't use what they never hear about.
principles.quote: إذا لم أخبر الناس عنه، فلن يذهب الناس إلى التطبيق ولن يرى أحد الأجزاء الأفضل.

principles.text: Results are lumpy and follow Pareto: half of the $30K came from the last 2 of 12 months.
principles.quote: من أصل الـ 30 ألف دولار تلك، جاء نصفها في الشهرين الماضيين.

sources.title: Day 3 of building Doof: vibe coding a food diary app with Cursor and a coin-flip anti-craving feature
sources.originalTitle: day 3 of building a viral mobile app in 30 days - vibe coding to $10k mrr
sources.summary: Jack live-streams vibe coding his mobile food diary app (Doof) in React Native/Expo using Cursor. He shows how he prompts AI to fix bugs, picks models that stay on task, and designs a coin-flip feature to stop cravings. He also shares his plan for organic-only marketing and a hard paywall.

principles.text: Build the app you personally need. Solving your own problem gives clear scope and taste.
principles.quote: basically I wanted this for myself because I kept eating chocolate and chocolate usually makes me my head hurt if I track this in an app and I had a diary of all the things I ate that made my head hurt I could then not eat them as often

principles.text: If you can't code, start by prompting an AI builder like v0 or bolt.new, then learn by following along and reading docs.
principles.quote: if you have an idea plug it into some type of AI chat or system like vo or bolt and then see what it tells you to do see what it gives you and then just go from there and slowly try to learn what you're doing

principles.text: Feed AI the actual documentation: paste the full docs page, since it often won't follow links.
principles.quote: I put the documentation into cursor for Expo SQ light and then I also copy pasted the whole page and also fed that in because it usually doesn't read the links I send and then it did it all for me

principles.text: A smarter model isn't always better; pick the one that does only what you asked, since scope creep costs time.
principles.quote: I'm not using Cloud 3.7 because it usually adds like seven extra features and I just wanted to do the one thing I asked

principles.text: Charge for core features. Free versions don't earn money, so put the paywall in front of the core value.
principles.quote: they won't be able to actually use these core features without paying U sorry but I have made free stuff before and it I mean no one pays so trying to be profitable business here

principles.text: Market with fully organic social using your own tools, spending no money at first; consider influencers later.
principles.quote: I'm going to use postbridge which is my app but I'm going to Market it mainly through or or all through organic social so I'm not going to spend any money eventually maybe hire influencers but at first just everything fully organic

sources.title: How Jack Friks gets 1,000+ free app downloads: warm new accounts, post value-first short video
sources.originalTitle: how to get 1000 downloads to your b2c app for $0 this month - day 8/30 building a viral mobile app
sources.summary: Jack explains his organic social playbook for B2C apps, drawn from getting his earlier app to 100k downloads. Warm up a fresh account by scrolling only in-niche content, post manually and slowly, recreate proven viral formats as value-first content (never ads), and convert through comments.

principles.text: Use a brand new account and warm it up 15 minutes a day for 2-3 days before posting anything.
principles.quote: if your account is not warm it doesn't matter how good your content is it will not get reach and you need reach and we need it free

principles.text: While warming up, only engage with content in your niche so the algorithm learns your audience.
principles.quote: the algorithm will push your videos out to your audience based on what you watch

principles.text: Never make a straight ad. Give value first (laugh, feel seen, information) and put the app in the caption or comments.
principles.quote: never make an ad ads do not perform they don't go viral you have to make something that first gives value to the person watching it

principles.text: Post slowly and manually at first: about one video a day, spaced hours apart. Spamming gets you zero reach.
principles.quote: if your account is new I would only post one every 24 hours if you want to really go fast and crazy half the time you're going to end up getting zero views on all of your accounts

principles.text: Recreate formats you have seen work instead of starting from scratch, and keep milking a format while it still works.
principles.quote: don't just start from scratch look at things you've seen work that have a lot of traction and then recreate those

principles.text: Marketing is most of the game for app revenue, so spend your time on distribution, not just building.
principles.quote: 90% of the game of making money in the App Store is getting people to download your app not if your app's actually really good but if it has interest

sources.title: Day 9/30: Rebuilding a mobile app onboarding with a hard paywall and vibe coding
sources.originalTitle: day 9/30 building a viral mobile app to $1000 - revamping onboarding with vibe coding
sources.summary: Jack live-streams revamping the onboarding of his food-mood app Doof after weak trial conversions. He moves to a hard, non-dismissible paywall, lengthens onboarding with personalization and feature carousels, and uses Figma mockups fed to Cursor to build it. He studies competitor onboardings and iterates copy many times.

principles.text: Sell users on results before the paywall; don't assume they'll pay before being told what they get.
principles.quote: we have to sell that we can't just assume that they're going to believe uh that they're just going to walk into the app and pay us money before we tell them anything about results and what they want

principles.text: A longer onboarding makes users invest time, so they're more likely to pay at the paywall.
principles.quote: once they get to the pay wall they've already been in this sequence of onboarding for quite some time they're going to be more likely to pay cuz they have put in a cost which is their time

principles.text: Use a hard gated paywall and state clearly in the App Store description that content requires a paid subscription.
principles.quote: you put a disclaimer in your description and you make it abundantly clear that there is paid content this is it requires a paid subscription

principles.text: Remove free trials first to measure true onboarding conversion, then A/B test trials back in.
principles.quote: you want to get the true conversion first then AB tested super important

principles.text: Show real app screenshots and features in onboarding so users see how it solves their problem before paying.
principles.quote: this is going to tell them and show them aha that's how we do it right away

principles.text: Good copy takes many iterations; write about ten versions of each headline and pick the best.
principles.quote: you're going to have to iterate through like 10 different versions like I had like 10 different versions of each of these slides

sources.title: How Jack Friks makes a viral food-diary app video live: recreate a proven format in CapCut for $0
sources.originalTitle: day 11/30 building a viral mobile app - making content to drive downloads ($0)
sources.summary: Day 11 of building a mobile app: Jack live-streams making a short TikTok/Instagram video to drive downloads. He finds a proven format by scrolling his niche, recreates it with free AI images and CapCut, adds a call to action in the caption and pinned comment, and tests new formats daily.

principles.text: Find a format that already worked in your niche and recreate it instead of inventing content from scratch.
principles.quote: first I'm finding a format that has done well recreating it and then doing that every day trying different formats until something does better than the others and then I just reuse that format and repeat

principles.text: Warm up a new account by scrolling and engaging in your niche before posting.
principles.quote: when I've been scrolling to warm up these accounts cuz I didn't post for the first two days new account no posting I'm scrolling in my Niche finding videos that I can recreate liking them commenting following those accounts

principles.text: Don't expect an overnight hit; volume across formats raises your odds.
principles.quote: obviously we're not going to get a million views overnight although it can happen un likely but if we keep making videos it becomes more likely

principles.text: Put a call to action in the caption and top comment so views turn into downloads.
principles.quote: make sure the top comment is going to be for that is going to be saying like hey download the app

principles.text: AI-generated content needs curation; unfiltered slop doesn't get views.
principles.quote: making videos like this you do have to curate you can't just put out slop as slop I mean doesn't get views for a good reason

principles.text: Shadow-ban risk mostly comes down to acting like a real user on the platform.
principles.quote: Shadow Banning is kind of a thing but it's more or less if you're not acting like a human you're going to get less reach so act like a human that's the main thing

sources.title: Just do 100 reps: how repetition makes you prolific and good at anything
sources.originalTitle: just do 100 reps (getting your sh*t out to be prolific)
sources.summary: Jack argues the simplest way to improve at or test any pursuit is to do it 100 times. Volume increases your odds of hitting something good, and you can stop early if you learn you don't like it. He applies it to his own 1,200 videos and book-writing.

principles.text: To get better at something or learn if you want to do it, just do it 100 times.
principles.quote: إذا أردت أن تتحسن في شيء ما، أو أن تكتشف ما إذا كنت ترغب حقاً في فعله، فقم بأدائه 100 مرة.

principles.text: Output is a numbers game: more attempts raise your odds of a standout result.
principles.quote: أنت فقط تزيد من احتمالاتك. أنت تلعب لعبة الأرقام.

principles.text: Nobody succeeds overnight; the simple answer is repeating the thing many times.
principles.quote: معظم الناس لم يحققوا النجاح بين عشية وضحاها. لا أحد فعل ذلك تقريبًا.

principles.text: You don't need 100 reps of everything; a few reps tell you if you like it or should stop.
principles.quote: لست مضطراً للقيام بـ 100 تكرار لكل ما تبدأ به. يمكنك القيام بخمسة، ثلاثة، أو عشرة.

principles.text: Iterate on many versions and pick the last one, since it likely includes the improvements.
principles.quote: اختر العنوان رقم 400 لأنه على الأرجح نتاج التكرار.

principles.text: Early output will be mostly junk, but doing volume surfaces the gems and gradual progress.
principles.quote: في بعض ذلك الهراء ، توجد بعض الكنوز. هناك بعض الماس الخام.

sources.title: Escaping the attention economy: rest your brain so your curiosity can show you what you want
sources.originalTitle: If you give me 12 minutes of your attention, I'll give your life direction back
sources.summary: Jack argues that platforms profit from screen time over your lifetime, so regaining direction starts with knowing what you want out of life. His method is daily quiet time and boredom, which opens a "curiosity intake" that points you toward genuine interests you can pursue and act on.

principles.text: Platform incentives favor your screen time over your life, so don't expect them to give your attention back.
principles.quote: the incentives of making money for many platforms including the one you're watching this on right now are more incentivized for screen time than lifetime

principles.text: To escape the attention loop, you must know what you want out of life; it makes putting the phone down easier.
principles.quote: if you do end up figuring out what you want out of life makes it way easier to keep going it makes it way easier to shut off your phone

principles.text: Start by doing nothing: daily quiet time lets your brain process accumulated information and clears the clutter.
principles.quote: the first step is actually counterintuitive you do nothing and what I mean by do nothing is genuinely you do nothing you sit there and you let your brain run wild

principles.text: Boredom opens a 'curiosity intake', giving you interests that come from your own head rather than an algorithm.
principles.quote: if you can allow yourself to be bored then this curiosity intake will open up and what this does and how it helps you is it gives you something that you can question and dive into deeper that is organically from your own head

principles.text: Clarity on what you want comes from acting and reflecting on what you did and didn't like, and it can change.
principles.quote: you're going to figure it out more and more as you introspect and look back on what you did and didn't like

principles.text: Define the primal emotion behind your goals and focus on it while doing the work that gets you there.
principles.quote: decide also why you want that what is the Primal emotion that that is going to bring to you

sources.title: How Jack Friks built Postbridge by scratching his own itch and staying simple
sources.originalTitle: Jack Friks interview transcript (Bootstrapped Founder)
sources.summary: Jack explains how he built Postbridge, a simple social scheduler, for himself after expensive bloated tools frustrated him. He covers building in public as a journal, keeping a product lean, word-of-mouth through genuine value, and staying skeptical of AI in content and product.

principles.text: Build the tool for yourself first; simple and useful for you often turns out useful for others.
principles.quote: when I made it for myself, I made it, like, as simple as possible and as useful as possible for me, which turned out to be very useful for other people.

principles.text: In a red ocean, don't fight on small feature comparisons; offer real value at a fair price and let pricing and features speak.
principles.quote: my angle was just to make something that really gives people a valuable like, something of value for a very fair price.

principles.text: Do something interesting, then document it; followers become a byproduct of building the business, not the goal.
principles.quote: I post, I do something, I post, I do something, and it grows my business. And then as a byproduct, it grows my followers

principles.text: Use your own product daily and market it with proof of how you used it; a useful pinned tweet drives product adoption.
principles.quote: I use PostBridge to post the content to make it easier. This is exactly how I did it. It's literally my pinned tweet.

principles.text: Keep the product lean by filtering every feature on whether it bloats things for a first-time user.
principles.quote: Is this something that is going to bloat the software and make it less valuable to, like, a normal first time user?

principles.text: Keep what works until results actually stop; people abandon formats from boredom before performance drops.
principles.quote: But if you have something that works, you keep using it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack Friks explains his organic social playbook for driving app downloads for free: new niche-only accounts, a week of warm-up, one post a day, copying proven formats, and iterating until something hits. He stresses relevance to the product and clear calls to action over raw views.

chunks.heading: Starting organic social from zero: new account, warm-up week, and posting cadence
chunks.text:
Jack markets his mobile apps with organic short-form video on Instagram and TikTok and spends $0 on ads. He says he never had money for ads and did not like them. He started with zero followers on every page and has repeated the process on multiple pages for the same app.

His account setup rules:
- Create a brand new account for each business or app.
- Use that account only to scroll and follow content in the niche, so the algorithm knows who to push your first posts to.
- Post nothing for the first week. He used to say 2-3 days but now says a full week, so the algorithm does not read the account as a bot.
- After the warm-up, post one video a day. If posting several, space them at least 3-4 hours apart.
- Post manually. He runs a social media scheduling tool and still tells people not to use it on new accounts until they are warmed up.
- A properly warmed account should get hundreds of views per video. If it does not, "something is wrong" and he would stop posting and fix it. Without warm-up you post "videos to the void".

Why a fresh account beats an old one: on a personal account that posts off-topic content, Instagram shows the video to the existing audience first. If they do not engage, it is not pushed further. A new account tests across many audiences and has wide reach potential.

chunks.heading: Finding content formats: scroll your niche, save, and recreate
chunks.text:
Jack's first step in organic social is finding ideas, and he says it is not hard.

- Scroll the niche on the new account and click save on videos that are already viral for the target audience.
- Look at the saved videos when it is time to create.
- Look for formats that are simple and low effort. Many videos are full productions, and you do not need one.
- Set a timer for 10 minutes a day. He says you will get the hang of what goes viral in a week or two.
- He has not been able to use AI to find formats and does not think this is outsourceable yet.

His example, a "Curiosity Quench" page for hobbies and anti-doom-scrolling:
- He saw a 2x2 image video with around a million likes.
- He first tried "things to do instead of scrolling" and it did not work.
- He iterated to hobbies. One post hit about 10k views, when he had been stuck below 1,000.
- He remade it and one post reached about 100k views.
- He then moved the same format to a food app, made 30 posts, and one hit about 2 million views.
- He now posts only that one format, a 2x2 image grid with a caption. He found it after making "hundreds of videos".
- He keeps using a format as long as it still gets results, even if he has used it many times.

Formats transfer across niches. A format validated in one niche can be applied to another, but you still scroll your own niche on a new account so the algorithm knows your audience.

chunks.heading: Testing and iteration: volume, angles, and patience
chunks.text:
- Jack tests one new piece of content a day when trying new formats, and iterates on what works.
- Usually it takes 30 to 100 posts before something does well. In his example, hits came after roughly 30 to 40 tries.
- The common pitfall is making the same video over and over and expecting a different result. Each post should change an angle.
- If a post hits 10,000 or 100,000 views on the first try, keep doing that.
- Expect a month or two of work before real results, especially the first time.
- Views do not convert directly to signups. Converting attention is a separate skill.
- Start manually. Use CapCut as the simplest editing tool. "If you can't do it manually, there's no point of automating it", because you will not know what works. He suggests worrying about automation after about 100 pieces of content.
- Once he found a working format, he automated the 2x2 grid image generation with an assistant he built and is working on producing it in bulk.

Jack's 80/20 as summarized with the host: find the format, pick the niche, and post consistently.

chunks.heading: Making organic content that drives signups, not just views
chunks.text:
Jack says getting views is not the goal. Views must go to the business, so content has to be highly relevant to what is being promoted.

Why people get "100k views but two signups":
- The video has no call to action.
- The pinned comment does not say to go download the app for a specific result.
- The main caption does not tell people to download it, say what it is called, or give the website link.

His tactics:
- Put the call to action in the caption and pinned comment. "You have to kind of spam it in their face."
- It does not need to be in the video.
- Do not make the content look like an ad. That is the "biggest mistake" in organic content. If it looks like an ad, people scroll and the algorithm gives it about 20 views.
- Make content people engage with. The algorithm pushes posts further when people comment or rewatch.

chunks.heading: Comment-to-DM automation with ManyChat
chunks.text:
Jack had tried ManyChat before he saw social success and disabled it. He now thinks he overlooked it.

- The pattern is "comment X and I'll DM you a link" to the app, tool or guide.
- He says it is a big deal especially for B2B things, tools and guides.
- It is probably not important until you have a working piece of content that catches. Once you have a working system or content, it "could be huge".
- Comments are also a strong algorithm signal.

chunks.heading: Using AI to generate content ideas once you have a format
chunks.text:
Jack's view is that AI helps after you have a working format, but does not replace scrolling to find one.

- He tested it live: describe the app (a food diary app), explain the format that gets views, and ask for more low-effort video format ideas related to the app.
- Output he found usable: split-screen or swipe comparisons such as how you feel after a bagel versus oatmeal, "foods that secretly drain you", underrated snack ideas, and "foods that make you smart or dumb" shown with app logs.
- Output he rejected: ideas that read like ads, such as "What I logged today in the app".
- Copy is the hardest part. Tell AI to write like Gen Z and use lowercase so it does not read as AI.
- AI is not autonomous. You need a sense of what works, which comes from scrolling about 10 minutes a day for a week.
- He had not used ChatGPT for ideation as much as he should, and says it can bridge the gap between seeing a format and adapting it to your app.

chunks.heading: Attention first, then conversion
chunks.text:
- Jack frames it as two skills: get attention in a niche, then convert that attention into people using the SaaS or mobile app.
- He says the skill transfers to any business, though consumer-facing products are easier.
- The numbers: he went four or five years making basically nothing before reaching about $10-20k a month, and "it all happens really fast" when it does.
- He says anyone can do this because it is accessible and content takes little to make, but you have to do it longer than you expect and develop a system.
- He keeps a pinned guide on Twitter covering warm-up and common pitfalls, and tells people to reread it when unsure.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack Friks explains how he went from eight months of near-zero revenue to a $15k month and a 100k-download app by scrolling his niche daily and copying formats that already work. He also covers building on proven niches, testing paywalls, staying solo and profitable, and turning down a $1M offer because he enjoyed the work.

chunks.heading: Jack's method for finding organic TikTok/Instagram formats: scroll, save, copy
chunks.text:
- Jack found the format for his Curiosity Quench app (a stop-scrolling app) "by consistently scrolling every morning." He argues you can't figure out a platform "just posting and not being on the platform. You have to be a user."
- Early routine: about an hour a day on marketing, which meant scrolling his branded page or a page in his niche to see what goes viral, then making one different video. He did this for roughly 100-200 days with little result before one format hit.
- Current routine:
  - Set a 15-minute timer and scroll TikTok and Instagram.
  - Use the save feature to bookmark formats.
  - Later, set aside 30 minutes to an hour to make a video from the saved material.
- He says he finds a "gem" nearly every session, though sometimes it turns out to be 8 months old and stale. He can still learn from videos in unrelated niches by borrowing the structure (a listicle, a 6-second background clip with a caption overlay).
- His principle: "If you can try to get some of what's working for an existing viral video rather than starting over from scratch, I think that's the best way to go." Remaking a proven format also takes far less effort than inventing a new one.
- He credits a daily habit with training his brain to see content ideas everywhere: set time aside for the goal and "now my brain is going to be thinking about this even when I'm not in that set aside time."
- He says some days he posts a bad video anyway, and sometimes those do well.

chunks.heading: Curiosity Quench: 400 copies of one slideshow format, $15K peak month
chunks.text:
- Curiosity Quench gives people action plans to pursue hobbies instead of doom scrolling. It took about 8 months to make real money, with 50-60 downloads a day before the viral format. Jack says the lesson was "downloads don't equal money."
- Peak: $15,000 in one month. September 2024 was the second-highest month and October 2024 the next.
- Format: he saw an Instagram video with about 1M views showing four pictures and a funny caption ("most attractive hobbies"), unrelated to any app. He swapped in hobbies and pictures from his app (widgets) and changed the caption.
- He made that video about 400 times. After the first ~100 he saw it getting a lot of views and kept going.
- Call to action: he put the download link in a comment and pinned it early. People commented angrily on the hobby lists, which drew attention to his pinned comment.
- Roughly every 20 videos he put the app in one of the pictures. Some of those reached millions of views and brought thousands of downloads.
- Results: a day with 2M views and about 1,000 downloads, versus his earlier 50-60 a day. The format ran about a year and slowed around 3 months after the peak. By the interview it was "milk dry": "golden geese don't last forever."
- Trade-off he describes: a video can get 10,000 views and 1,000 downloads, or 3M views and 100 downloads. He keeps posting anything that consistently brings in some downloads.
- Limits: attribution is nearly impossible. He had no idea how many downloads a given 1.8M-view video produced.
- He runs the same format across several accounts and reposts to TikTok, Shorts and Instagram.

chunks.heading: Paywalls and monetization lessons from his first app
chunks.text:
- The first monetization was confusing "quench credits" and a shop where users had to find premium access themselves. Few people bought.
- He added a paywall with RevenueCat first, but it was clunky and he couldn't customize it. Then he migrated to Superwall.
- Revenue went from about $500-$1,000 a month (over roughly 5 months) to $2,000-$4,000 a month after 3-4 months of testing on Superwall.
- What changed:
  - Realizing paywalls and free trials are the standard. Before, he didn't know.
  - Testing headers and copy.
  - Gating certain features.
- He used Superwall's templates and only added his logo and colors. He says "templates are really good, so I mostly just use those." A paywall takes about 5 minutes on a new app. Looking legit increases the chance someone buys.
- Doof (a food diary app) used a template paywall too, without much thought.
- On Lovely, he switched from a hard paywall to freemium after bad reviews and because he wanted friends to use it.

chunks.heading: Lovely: Twitter launch, a viral grocery list and 100K downloads in about 10 weeks
chunks.text:
- Lovely is a couples app. A doodle or love note appears on a partner's home screen widget. He made it for himself and his fiancée, and a friend suggested it.
- Launch tweet: he said he'd work on the app for the rest of the year and take it from $0 to $5,000 a month in about 10 weeks. He quote-tweeted it about six times with updates and context, and each one got more views.
  - Two hooks: the build-in-public story of making $5,000 a month, and the novelty of love notes on a home screen.
- A user replaced a love note with a grocery list. That tweet got 16M views and 33,000 likes. Jack added context in a quote tweet reading roughly "I made this app, someone's now using it as a grocery list," which got 300,000 likes and about 40,000 downloads overnight.
- Russian news picked it up, which brought about 10,000 downloads from Russia the next day. Another tweet later reached about 20M views.
- Twitter plus Russian news added about $2,000-$3,000 MRR before he posted on TikTok.
- Totals: about 102,000 users, about 10,000 paying, and roughly $4,200 MRR, against his $5,000 goal.
- He kept adding context in follow-up posts, which created "a neverending cycle of interesting things that are happening and they're all about this app."

chunks.heading: Lovely video formats: from 150K views and ~100 downloads to a format converting about 20x better
chunks.text:
- TikTok started about a week after the tweets. He posted once a day from a burner phone with a VPN and tried new formats found by scrolling his niche.
- First attempt: a relationship-themed TikTok that hit 150K views but brought only about 100-200 downloads. He calls it "silver or copper," with lots of views and little conversion.
- Winning format:
  - He saw a competitor couples app posting a shared-whiteboard-style video that was doing well on TikTok.
  - He built it as a presentation mode of his existing shared whiteboard feature in a day and posted videos the next day.
  - The fifth video reached 490,000 views. He scaled from 1 a day to 2 and then 3 a day.
  - On Instagram the first one got 300,000 views and several reached millions within two weeks.
- Format: an 8-10 second screen recording of him using the app, ending by showing the app. It converted "like 20 times better" than the two-by-two slideshows.
- He did not analyze why it worked: "I knew if it's going viral for them, I can make it go viral for me." He says TikTok and Instagram rarely correlate, so you test on both.
- Principle: videos that look organic but show the app are "gold," versus the "silver" of unrelated meme formats.
- Doof used the old slideshow format and got one 5M-view video that drove a bunch of downloads, which he says shows "all it really takes is one good video." He still thinks going mega-viral without mentioning the app is worth trying, but should not be the only bet.

chunks.heading: Building apps: copy proven niches, build for yourself, bet on frames
chunks.text:
- Idea rule: everything he's built "has a successful counterpart." He builds a personal version of something that already works and takes marketing cues from existing apps in that niche.
- He builds what he wants to exist (Curiosity Quench, Doof, Lovely). Doof was a 30-day challenge to go from zero to $1,000, which he hit in the first month using Instagram, TikTok and Twitter.
- He thinks "the idea is the biggest part" and any app can be made interesting by how it's framed.
- Buyer insight on couples apps: if a girlfriend asks her boyfriend to buy the app, he'll probably pay, and two users enjoying it together are more likely to talk about it.
- He keeps his marketing from looking like ads: people won't watch ads, so consumer app content should look organic.
- On early failures: before coding, he spent about 3 years on print-on-demand, Amazon KDP, crypto and newsletters. The lesson was to make things for himself and then work out how to bring people to them, and that a business has to solve a problem.
- Advice: "Get it out there and see what happens. Start making videos... you're going to be 10 times ahead of the person who's been sitting on their hands."

chunks.heading: PostBridge, the $1M offer he turned down, and staying small
chunks.text:
- He built PostBridge, a simple social scheduling tool (upload a video, post to all channels), because posting by hand took about an hour a day. Batching content for a week or two cut it to about 10 minutes of work.
- It took off immediately after launch and displaced the mobile app he was working on.
- In April (of the prior year), Sahil from Gumroad tweeted an offer of $1 million for it. At the time PostBridge was making about $12,000 a month and growing 30-40% per month. Jack declined because he was having fun and it was at its high. It was still making about $20K MRR at the time of the interview.
- He weighs fun heavily: "if I'm going to be working for myself and building, I want to make sure it's enjoyable." He accepts some apps may make less (for example, not using hard paywalls).
- Stance: he wants to stay solo and very small, so "profitability is the number one metric to be able to keep going." His mindset hasn't changed since earning money, only less stress.
- Scaling Lovely: the app is premium so paid ads don't make sense (he hasn't used them). He reinvested about $1,000 to hire people found through Twitter and word of mouth to post the winning format across 20-40 accounts, aiming for hundreds of videos a day. He says it's still in the testing phase, with Instagram the best bet.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack Friks explains how he drove 100,000+ free downloads to his mobile app by posting non-salesy short-form content on Instagram and TikTok, with the call to action only in the caption and pinned comment. He also covers validating ideas through organic media before building, and how this led him to build Post Bridge to schedule and template content at scale.

chunks.heading: Validate with media before building the product
chunks.text:
- Jack's core idea: the best way to validate a product is to build the media first and see if people want it, before building the product.
- Anyone can build an app now, so the hard question is whether people want it and whether it can be distributed.
- He validated his first mobile app this way. Day one, he posted a video mocking up a solution to "I'm stuck on my phone all day". It got about 2,000 views and 10 comments.
- He kept posting. About 10 videos later, an AI-generated mockup video got about 30,000 views.
- He then made a sign-up page and got about 1,000 users to the web app in the first month and a half, even though "it was so bad".
- His view: if a content format with your problem as the hook can't go viral organically, the pain probably isn't big enough to build a business on. The bigger the pain, the more organic potential.
- He suggests organic social can validate the idea with just a Figma screenshot or mockup.

chunks.heading: The "media as vehicle, caption as call to action" model
chunks.text:
- Jack's rule: don't make the content an ad. Organic ads get roughly 100-200 views every time.
- The less call to action in the video, the better the views. A few viral pieces lift the whole account and boost its other videos.
- His top format is a 6-second, four-image post with no call to action in the video. The app promotion lives only in the caption and the pinned comment.
- That one template drove about 50,000 downloads. Videos hit 1 to 5 million views, and some days brought thousands of downloads.
- He says he was often too lazy to even comment. The caption alone did the work.
- Content must still be related to the app. Putting the app in one of the four images has also reached a million views, but it is less likely to go "way viral", because people dislike ads on their for-you page.
- Mixing in a little salesy content works once the account has real reach and isn't stuck at 200-view walls.

chunks.heading: Finding viral formats
chunks.text:
- His process is not very tactical. He scrolls an Instagram account that follows only his target niche, then likes and comments on videos.
- He looks at what drove the comments, why people watched to the end, and whether it can be replicated as a format.
- If it can, he saves it to a folder and recreates it in CapCut or another short-form editor. If it works, he turns it into a template.
- He started by testing about 50+ formats before landing on one that hit a million views.
- Engagement angles that worked: relatable ("that's me") posts and deliberately outrage-bait ones, such as misspelling "astrology" and "astronomy" so people argue in the comments. He has cooled on the outrage angle.
- If a niche has no established format, he says you can still find an angle. Post two a day for about two months and test hundreds of videos.
- Misses are part of it. Many people quit because the numbers game is discouraging.

chunks.heading: Scaling volume across accounts and platforms
chunks.text:
- Jack's limit on scale is how many videos you can make and how many warmed-up accounts you can post to.
- Accounts must be warmed up. They should have been used like a human, so they aren't suppressed at 200 views a video.
- His rough rule at the time was about 3 videos per account, spaced 3-4 hours apart, divided across the number of accounts.
- He posts the same media to all channels but optimizes for one. He targets Instagram because he scrolls it and finds formats there.
- Nearly 99% of his views for the four-image format came from Instagram. TikTok gave only some extra views.
- He advises one channel at a time. In 2025 it is free to cross-post to the others, and he has not opened TikTok in about three months while it still brought thousands of downloads.
- Pick the channel where your buyer actually spends time.

chunks.heading: Funnel and product fit
chunks.text:
- The funnel worked well because it pointed at a mobile app, which is easy to reach from mobile video. Jack estimates a web app would get about 10% of the conversions.
- He still thinks the approach works for web apps, just less efficiently.

chunks.heading: Turning an internal tool into Postbridge
chunks.text:
- Jack built his own scheduler, Postbridge, because competitors charged about $50 a month for the number of accounts he managed, and he "just hates spending money".
- He posted a tweet teaser with a UI screenshot saying he was working on something cool. It got about 1,000 likes and 200,000 impressions, and someone said he should sell it.
- He added a creative section to make videos and templates inside the tool. At the time it had only three templates, and finding viral formats was the part he was focusing on.
- Results at the time: about 4,000 videos created in a month and a half, with roughly 300 customers.
- The mobile app's growth funded the idea, and Postbridge now makes more than the mobile app that it scaled.

chunks.heading: Building and what to build
chunks.text:
- His build advice: start with any AI helper (Cursor, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT), get a prototype out, and don't overthink it.
- He thinks mobile apps are not much harder than web apps. The costs are the lag before results, store review, and no live users right away.
- He believes web and B2B is easier for a solo founder to make substantially more money on.
- He builds what he needs for himself. Both of his main ideas worked out, so the hit rate from "build for myself" has been high.
- His plan is to polish Postbridge, then use it to promote other mobile apps or scale one very far.
- He is skeptical of paid ads personally and has leaned organic because it is free to start. He says that is a personal preference and acknowledges paid ads work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack explains how he built PostBridge, a simple social scheduler, because existing tools were too expensive and bloated for posting short videos for his app. He covers building in public without chasing followers, staying kind, keeping a product lean, and avoiding AI for content to keep an authentic voice.

chunks.heading: Why Jack built PostBridge: scratching his own itch in a red ocean
chunks.text:
- Jack built PostBridge in October (about 7 months before the interview) because existing social schedulers were "too expensive" and had "too many features."
- He made it as simple and useful as possible for himself, and it turned out to be useful for others too. He says he didn't expect it to do as well as it did.
- Arvid describes it as a business doing roughly $13-18k a month and helping thousands of creators and founders. Jack didn't confirm a specific figure himself.
- The problem it solved: posting the same short video to Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Twitter, Bluesky and more meant manual uploads on each. PostBridge saves him 10-20 minutes per video per day.
- He acknowledges that building for yourself "doesn't solve everything" because you could build something only three other people want. In his case the market was bigger.

chunks.heading: Competing in a crowded market with simplicity, fair pricing and a point of view
chunks.text:
- The space is a red ocean with many similar tools. Jack doesn't compete on small feature-by-feature claims ("this is better, that's better").
- His angle: "something of value for a very fair price." He points people to the pricing page and features, because the tool does similar things and works.
- He uses his own tool daily, so he is incentivized to improve it for a specific persona. The current persona is mobile app founders.
- His pinned tweet explains exactly how he grew a mobile app with organic content using PostBridge. It is one of his most popular tweets because it is genuinely useful, and people then go and use the tool.
- Word of mouth has gone further than with anything he has built before: "people appreciate that a lot and they share with their friends."

chunks.heading: Keeping a product lean as a solo founder
chunks.text:
- Main filter: build for what he uses day to day and ask "how can this make my day simpler and easier?"
- He adds a feature if it is reasonable and won't add a complex workflow.
- With every change he asks whether it will bloat the software and make it less valuable to a normal first-time user.
- Core positioning is "as simple as possible." If a feature keeps the product simple, he adds it.
- Next focus is content generation, which he treats as almost its own product. It is an input stream into the tool and adds optionality without making the base tool more complex.
- He has no AI tooling inside PostBridge, which keeps it "bare bones."

chunks.heading: Marketing mobile apps with daily organic video
chunks.text:
- His earlier app, Curiosity Quench (an anti-scrolling app), reached about 60,000 downloads, largely from organic short videos.
- Workflow: make a roughly 6-second video, then post it to Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Twitter and Bluesky at the same time.
- After finding a video format that worked well, he automated it. In PostBridge you upload the basic parts of a template and it outputs the video.
- He now makes the template-based video every day, uploads it to all channels for his app and runs it close to autopilot.
- The irony that started it: promoting an app meant to reduce scrolling required him to scroll while manually posting. PostBridge let him post without opening the "suck you in" apps. He doesn't open Instagram or TikTok for months at a time.
- He treats time saved as the highest-impact kind of product value.

chunks.heading: Planned content generation: guided templates, not done-for-you AI
chunks.text:
- Vision: templates that have produced results, instructions on how to use them, and guidance on evoking an emotional reaction from the target audience, with ideas per niche.
- Goal: help businesses drive organic growth and get users to their product.
- Reasoning: if the scope is too narrow or too wide, "no one knows where to start." He wants to provide a starting point, "not done for you completely, but like a guided approach."
- Formats go stale at different rates by platform, so he says you should always be iterating.
- Observation on iteration: a video format may work for 5 months or a year, but most people drop it because it feels repetitive, even while it still works. His rule: if it works, keep using it; when it stops, iterate until you find something that works again.
- The product aims to help people find what is current. He says he won't do it perfectly but will try.

chunks.heading: Building in public: do things, then talk about them
chunks.text:
- He says follower growth was never his goal. His goal was a valuable business, and he documents it on Twitter, which has about 40k followers.
- The sequence: do something, post about it, which grows the business, with followers as a byproduct. He contrasts this with people who try to grow followers to grow a business: "you can tell if somebody's really doing something or they're just tweeting aphorisms."
- He uses Twitter as a "personal public journal" and posts unfiltered stray thoughts. About half of them get no attention, and roughly a tenth are controversial or hit.
- He uses no AI for text posts.
- He is kind by choice. He tries to make his points objective and nice, believing people will be mad regardless but there is a nicer way to say things. As a result his replies are mostly friendly.
- His view on where social media is heading: because so much content is not human, honest, flawed, raw posting will stand out and build something valuable amid junk.
- Pitfall he names: the "monkey brain" urge to do things just so he can post about them. He tries to play the game in a way that also protects his mental health.

chunks.heading: Engagement, notifications and moderation
chunks.text:
- He engages mainly on Twitter and checks other platforms about once a week or month. Replying everywhere would be robotic and unsustainable, and "people realize you're a human" when you can't get to everything.
- All social notifications are off. His only push notifications are texts from a few people.
- He doesn't moderate content in PostBridge. Because it connects through official platform APIs, the platforms moderate themselves, and he trusts algorithms and people's own choices.

chunks.heading: Using AI to learn to code, and security lessons
chunks.text:
- Less than two years before the interview he didn't know how to code beyond basic HTML and CSS. He uses Cursor and calls AI a non-judgmental teacher for fast learning.
- Outside coding he mostly avoids AI, including for customer service and content, unless it is clearly very beneficial. He isn't against others using it.
- He was attacked twice in a few months, partly because he was a vocal proponent of vibe coding. No user data was harmed. The main cost was a bigger bill from his provider.
- He learned the security basics quickly and says you can "prompt your way to making something decently secure."
- His advice: if you handle customer information, take security seriously, because a breach can end the business overnight. Don't be paralyzed by fear, but know someone could attack you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack updates his 2-month push to build a $10k/month consumer app. A daily burner-phone TikTok routine found a replicable video format that drove 11,000 downloads in 48 hours. He then moved the app to freemium and plans to reinvest into UGC creator accounts to scale the format.

chunks.heading: How Jack found a TikTok format that drove 11,000 downloads in 48 hours (Lovely, week 6)
chunks.text:
- Context: Jack is running a public two-month challenge to take a consumer mobile app (Lovely, a couples app) to $10k/month. The target was originally $5,000/month, stretched to $10k.
- By week 6 the app had about 56,000 downloads. His launch tweet went viral and was picked up by Russian news, which brought about 3,000 downloads. A quote tweet a week and a half later brought about 40,000.
- Roughly 11,000 of those downloads came in the last 48 hours, from his organic TikTok and Instagram strategy.
- The first week of the TikTok effort gave minimal results. It took about a week and a half to find a working format, which he calls "exceptionally fast" and partly luck.
- At week 6 the app was at $3,194 MRR in USD (about $5,000 for him as a Canadian), about a month after he built it.

chunks.heading: The daily routine for finding formats on a burner TikTok account
chunks.text:
- He uses a burner phone with TikTok and a US VPN.
- Every morning he scrolls TikTok for a while on the new account, finds videos in his niche that already did well, saves them, and makes videos based on them.
- The goal is to find a format that works, not to reinvent the wheel: "You're not trying to recreate the wheel here."
- His written guide covers account creation, warm-up and content testing. The main step is finding videos in the niche by scrolling on a fresh account.
- Once a format is found, he no longer needs to search. He batch-records content (pre-recorded doodles) and posts three a day: morning, after lunch and after dinner.
- His plan is to "milk" the format until it is overused and stops working as well.

chunks.heading: The winning format: show a cool in-app feature, not an ad
chunks.text:
- The winning video shows the app's shared whiteboard feature, which looks like a lock screen and is used to send love notes from one phone to another. He copied this from another app in his niche.
- At first these videos got 1,000 to 2,000 views each, and one hit about 10k on Instagram. Later ones reached 500k, 120k, 100k and 90k views, and one on Instagram approached 2 million.
- Views are not the metric, downloads are. A different video got 200k views but only about 100 downloads. A 100k-view video in the winning format brought about 1,000 downloads.
- The app is visible in the video, but it is not an ad: the video shows a feature people want, and that is enough to get past the "this is an ad" reaction.
- Viewers who watch it are likely couples, which is the audience the app wants.
- The account had zero followers a week earlier and 1,500 after one video blew up. "All it really takes is one thing to blow up."
- He notes this applies to B2C mobile apps, not to B2B SaaS like his other product PostBridge, because SaaS is hard to make not look like an ad.

chunks.heading: Engagement tactic: deliberate misspellings
chunks.text:
- He put an on-purpose spelling mistake in a video's text because "everybody loves being right."
- The video drew 1,200 likes and many comments correcting the error.
- His reasoning: the algorithm rewards comments, since commenting means people are watching.

chunks.heading: Free app with premium features
chunks.text:
- He moved the app from paid to free, with premium features, and says it is better for the long term.
- Downloads now convert less (conversion and proceeds in the last 24 hours looked "terrible"), and he accepts that. "Slow is better" for when the money comes in; if the app is good, the money will come.
- Users who enjoy the app and leave a positive review feel better about paying.
- The model is common in the couples niche, and couples come back frequently. One partner will often buy a subscription and share it.
- He had about 150 monthly trials pending, which could be about $700 MRR in theory but is more likely $200 to $300. Users who do not convert right away may come back and convert later.

chunks.heading: Reinvestment plan to scale the format
chunks.text:
- Lovely had made about $7,000 USD over the last 90 days.
- He plans to put about $4,000 to $5,000 back into scaling the working format over the next month.
- The plan is 10 to 20 TikTok and Instagram accounts run by UGC creators (for example, girls' profile pictures), recording many videos with varied hooks, posting about three a day per account.
- He had done everything solo up to this point, including running PostBridge, and had not hired anyone.

chunks.heading: General playbook for a first $10k/month mobile app
chunks.text:
- He says growing an app is not easy now but very possible, especially B2C with a broad, helpful product.
- Getting to the first $10k/month on TikTok is "relatively simple": spend a lot of time on TikTok, find formats that already worked, recreate them so they relate to your app but don't read as an ad, and funnel downloads.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack built a Swift couples app in about 3 days using Claude Code in Cursor with no hand-written code, and launched it with a build-in-public tweet that drew half a million views. He explains his plan to scale it: find a short-form content format that converts, then automate posting.

chunks.heading: Idea-to-revenue in 5 days: the build timeline and results
chunks.text:
- Jack had the app idea on a Wednesday and the app went live on the App Store about 5 days later. It earned its first dollar the day before he recorded the video.
- It is a couples app: "love letters" sent to a partner that show up as home-screen widgets, plus check-ins, doodles and reminders. He built it for himself and his fiancée.
- The build took about 3 days at 6 to 8 hours a day.
- Jack says part of the speed was luck, and that the launch-day spike was a viral post and not yet a repeatable system.
- Launch results, 3 hours after going live: 100 downloads, 11 trial starts, and one yearly sub for $21 in profit.
- Results at recording: $42 in proceeds, 460 downloads, and 36 conversions (2 yearly subs, 34 trial starts).
- He estimates 50% or more of the trials had already canceled, leaving maybe 15 active trials at best.
- The trials are on a weekly plan at $4.99 USD a week.

chunks.heading: How Jack built a Swift iOS app without writing code
chunks.text:
- He used Xcode and Swift, with Claude Code running inside Cursor (he used it as the editor shell, not Cursor's own AI). The project directory sat in the left sidebar and he asked Claude to build things.
- It was his first time using Swift. He says he hit few problems he couldn't search up or ask Claude about.
- He wrote no code himself. He says Claude was very good at the UI and usually got things right on the first try.
- Tweaking was slower because every change needs a rebuild in Xcode. Widgets were buggy to add.
- He double-checked the Firebase security rules himself, so that only owners can access their own data.
- Without a Mac, he suggests Expo and React Native, which he has used for three other apps. He still recommends a physical iPhone for testing.
- Steps he gives for doing something similar:
  1. Create the project in Xcode first to get a base.
  2. Open the project directory in Cursor or Claude Code and ask it to build.
  3. Work in test mode with a test bundle at first.
  4. Later, ask Claude to help migrate off test mode and prepare for production. It gave him many steps.
- App Store review is a time sink. App screens take time, and rejection is likely if terms of service and privacy policy aren't set up properly. Jack passed first try because he had done it before.

chunks.heading: Launch tweet and building in public as distribution
chunks.text:
- His launch tweet got about half a million views, 1,000 likes and many replies. Jack says he has "quite a bit of followers" on Twitter.
- He credits it to posting about what he builds, which he does regularly because people find it interesting. He also tweeted the results 3 hours after launch.
- Twitter is not the target audience for a couples app, which fits Instagram and TikTok better. Even so, the Twitter followers drove the early downloads and trials.
- He says these numbers came from build-in-public posts and are probably not replicable in the same way.

chunks.heading: Jack's plan to grow beyond the launch spike: find a content format, then scale it
chunks.text:
- Step 1: test content formats on TikTok. Jack made couples content from his fiancée's account, which he had warmed up with two other TikToks, and she made one video about the app.
- A direct ad-style video probably won't go anywhere, because people recognize it as an ad and don't connect with it. His non-ad tests also didn't perform well yet, because none had gone viral.
- Step 2: once a format works, repeat it. His other app, Curiosity Quench, passed 100,000 downloads. One format on it brought in roughly 30,000 to 50,000 of those downloads and got millions of views across many simple videos.
- That format converted modestly because the call to action sat only in the caption, but he kept repeating it once it worked.
- Step 3: make sure the format converts to paying downloads, not just views. He notes this app's first TikTok did not do well on that.
- Step 4: scale with automation. Once content performs when posted manually, post once or twice a day to TikTok, Instagram and other platforms through PostBridge, the tool he built for scaling his own mobile apps.
- Formats decay. His Curiosity Quench format works less well now because he hasn't iterated on it and it has been "milked dry".
- He says this system has grown apps to $100,000 before, and that it applies to consumer mobile apps, not B2B, which he calls "a whole different monster". His pinned tweet has a detailed outline.

chunks.heading: Why he builds his own apps
