chunks.text: - Much of the project serves as a case study for PostBridge: "if I can't grow my own mobile app through PostBridge, how can I expect to help other people grow too?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Week-4 update on a couples app: a viral Twitter post drove about 30,000 downloads overnight and roughly $6k in proceeds, with $2,800 MRR. Jack admits the luck, then lays out a repeatable plan: copy proven short-video formats, double down on hits, automate posting, and make the app free to try for better ratings and word of mouth.

chunks.heading: Hitting $6k and $2.8k MRR in four weeks with a new couples app
chunks.text:
- Jack built a couples app (widget for sending love letters to a partner) from idea to first revenue in 5 days, including app store review.
- By week 4 it had about $6,000 in proceeds since release. He states this is in USD, after Apple's cut, minus about $100 in refunds.
- MRR was $2,800, roughly 400 active subscriptions at $5 a month. The paywall offered monthly or lifetime only; he removed weekly.
- Pre-viral downloads were around 10,000 (he is unsure whether it was 10,000 or 20,000). The app had a hard paywall throughout this period.
- His original goal was a $5,000/month app by end of year from zero. Total proceeds passed $5,000 within weeks, so he raised the target to $10,000/month, with $5,000 MRR by end of year.
- He openly says a large part of this was luck.

chunks.heading: How one viral tweet drove 14 million views and about 30,000 downloads
chunks.text:
- Someone quote-tweeted his launch, swapping the love note image for a grocery list: "Starts with love notes, then life kicks in."
- It blew up. Jack added context and tied it to the app; his own post got 327,000 likes and 14 million views.
- That brought roughly 30,000 additional downloads almost overnight, taking the app to about 40,000 total downloads.
- The 40,000 downloads made only $6,000, which he calls low for the volume. His earlier app made $15,000 from 30,000 downloads in a month, because that app was better set up for monetization.
- He expects not to get another random viral Twitter post, so he plans a repeatable organic content system instead.

chunks.heading: Moving from hard paywall to premium (freemium) to fix ratings and word of mouth
chunks.text:
- About a week after the viral post, he built a whole new version of the app and shipped it. He feared it would go badly.
- He made the app premium rather than hard-paywalled, changed the logo and the whole app scheme (not just a basic menu).
- Ratings rose from 2.9 to 4.2 in that week.
- His reasons: people rate five stars more readily when there is no hard paywall, and many Twitter followers rated five stars because they know him.
- Freemium helps word of mouth: someone can share the app with a friend or partner, who can try it without entering a credit card or going through "50 onboarding steps" to hit a hard paywall.
- His goal: "make a good app that people want to use and eventually pay for."
- Revenue per download should trend upward as he fine-tunes, tests and iterates.

chunks.heading: Using Twitter to document the build in public
chunks.text:
- Jack argues Twitter can be a great marketing channel. He used it to document everything: features being built, reviews arriving, what he is thinking and doing.
- He finds documenting fun, and the story ("the plot is getting thicker") is part of what draws attention.
- Example of real engagement: a user accidentally spent shared heart points on a pig skin and their girlfriend was annoyed. Jack refunded the points, locked the skin and fixed it. He took it as proof that people care about the in-app points and actually use the app.
- He says he fixed the app "like 17 times" in the first month.

chunks.heading: The plan to reach $10k/month through free organic video
chunks.text:
- Core claim: the first $10,000/month "can be attained for free for $0" with organic short-form video.
- Formula for content: it must be good, entertaining and tell a story, and use a proven format that other content has already used, adapted to his own app.
- Example tactic: a fun skit video where the app appears in the video without being explicitly mentioned.
- Step-by-step plan for the next month:
  1. Finish polishing the app and add sound effects and features his fiancee wants.
  2. Post daily videos on Instagram and TikTok, trying different formats and templates.
  3. When one hits 10,000+ views, double down and recreate it in different ways.
  4. Once it is rolling, automate posting with PostBridge (his own product) to free up time, since he is still running his main business.
- Precedent: a year earlier he used this approach to get 30,000 downloads in one month for free on another app, which netted $15,000 that month (pinned on his Twitter).
- No paid ads in the plan.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack Friks kicks off a 30-day mobile app challenge by scoping "Doof", a junk-food diary with a coin-flip feature, built around his own problem. He walks through his idea-scoping doc, hard paywall and local-data decisions, an Expo plus Superwall boilerplate, vibe coding in Cursor, and why marketing is most of the work.

chunks.heading: Start from a problem you personally have
chunks.text:
- Jack's rule for picking an app idea: solve your own problem. He calls it "the easiest way to build something that's going to sell" and "the easiest way to be a user and build things that your users want because you want it."
- His idea for the 30-day challenge was "Doof" ("food" backwards), a food diary to quit junk food. It came from his own habit of eating badly and feeling worse for it.
- His sanity check before building: "would I pay for this?" If not, other people probably won't, so don't build it. The exception is a problem you don't have yourself, but he suggests starting with one you do.
- He chose a health niche because it is evergreen: people always need health problems solved and will pay for it.
- He argues ideas are worth very little. "The idea is only a multiplier for how good you execute." He rated Doof "good, it's okay, not amazing", but good enough because he will be his own user.
- He publicly shared the idea and the scope document on day one. Copycats can't be stopped once an app is live anyway, and they won't market as well or be solving their own problem.

chunks.heading: Scoping the idea in a one-page document
chunks.text:
- Jack writes the idea down in a doc before building. The questions it answers:
  - What problem does it solve, and for whom?
  - How does it solve it?
  - Which 1-3 core features does it have?
  - What are the bonus features that would be nice to have?
  - What is the tech stack, onboarding and paywall approach?
- He feeds the doc into ChatGPT to flesh it out, and suggests the same for finding problems worth solving.
- Doof's two core features:
  - A food and mood log: what you ate, how it felt, and whether you regret it.
  - A coin flip with adjustable odds (e.g. 50/50) for foods you're tempted by, so there is a barrier before the junk food.
- Core assumption stated up front: the user already wants to change their eating habits. If they don't, the app isn't for them.
- The 30-day plan builds only the two core features. Bonus features come only if there is time.
- Timeline logic: get the app out within the first two weeks. App review takes days and he usually misses something, and warming up social accounts and marketing can take a week alone. Time to market matters more than extra features.

chunks.heading: Product and monetization decisions
chunks.text:
- Onboarding: always include one. Describe the problem, then slowly show how the app solves it, before the paywall. This matters especially for mobile apps.
- Paywall: a hard paywall with a 7-day free trial, no free version. "Pay to use or download or just delete the app."
- He says a hard paywall with a free trial "tends to convert much, much better into sales" than freemium. His other app, Curiosity Quench, is freemium, and Doof is deliberately different.
- Privacy-first, local-only data: no authentication and no cloud sync, with everything in a local database on the device.
  - He admits it is partly laziness.
  - He also frames it as a selling point, since many people value not having data stored anywhere but their own device. He cites the app Habit Kit doing the same.
  - Tradeoff: deleting the app loses the data.

chunks.heading: Tech stack and boilerplate workflow
chunks.text:
- Stack: React Native with Expo and React Navigation, which publishes to both iOS and Android. He will probably submit to Apple first, and may add Android since the code is the same.
- Payments: Superwall, which he says is the easiest to implement now (previously people combined it with RevenueCat). Superwall public API keys are fine to ship in the app, because environment keys can't be hidden in a built binary.
- He keeps a free boilerplate (shared in his Discord) with onboarding screens, a base layout, tabs and Superwall pre-integrated. Setup steps:
  - Clone the repo.
  - Delete the included iOS and Android build folders if they cause problems.
  - Install dependencies, then start with Expo.
  - Add your Superwall project's public API key.
- Cursor costs him about $30 a month, with occasional slow requests that he works around by doing something else while it answers. He has never connected his own API keys.

chunks.heading: Using Cursor to prototype fast, then scrapping the output
chunks.text:
- Demonstrated workflow:
  - Paste the whole app scope document into Cursor's agent chat.
  - Ask it to design the UX and UI for the two core features and restructure the tabs as it sees fit.
  - Result in about 20-30 minutes: a log screen, a coin toss screen and a history screen.
- He also puts the app information into Cursor rules so the model keeps the context.
- His typing tip: sloppy typos in prompts still work. "Type slop and it still comes out pretty good."
- His honest assessment of the output: "this is slop", with too much margin and old UI left over. It is useful for seeing a baseline, not for shipping.
- Next step he planned: sketch the real UX in Figma as a "sketch pad", define colour themes and copy, and delete the existing UI before asking Cursor for more changes, so it doesn't iterate on a bad base.
- Logging UX idea: a quick slider-style scale per question (from strongly disagree to strongly agree), so a food can be logged fast, with a dashboard of foods that made you feel good.
- Simulator limits: features like barcode scanning need a physical device, so he skipped them for now.

chunks.heading: Marketing plan and numbers
chunks.text:
- His view: "the marketing is like 75% of the work." You can build an amazing app, but without marketing you get no downloads, views or money.
- Plan: build the app, start marketing as soon as possible, and use Post Bridge (his own tool) to make and schedule the videos.
- Content formats he uses:
  - Simple 2x2 image-style videos from the content studio, made in a few minutes, which have reached millions of views.
  - Talking-head videos explaining how the app works, a few of which have passed a million views.
  - A branded page reusing one template. He cites about 600,000, 45,000 and 2.8 million views on three posts, and says it has diminishing returns from overuse, so he plans new templates.
- Account warm-up: make the account, warm it up, and look for viral videos for inspiration. He notes you may need a VPN depending on location, and he is lucky as a Canadian to get US reach. He planned to stream this later.
- Track record he cited:
  - Curiosity Quench: over 100,000 downloads using the guide pinned on his Twitter.
  - About 20,000 monthly active users.
  - Almost $1,500 last month with no recent marketing or coding, and several yearly subscriptions about to renew.
  - Post Bridge: about $113,000 CAD in the last month. He keeps working on it daily as his main business during the challenge.
- Building in public: he says SaaS can succeed without a personal brand (most aren't built in public), but putting your name out there is harder to skip and "claiming responsibility" helps.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack recounts earning about $500K from a crypto YouTube channel, an NFT sellout and mining, then losing most of it to crypto-denominated tax bills, developer costs and poor accounting decisions. He closes by pivoting to a topic he wants to work on long term, valuing what he does over how much he makes.

chunks.heading: Why Jack lost most of $500,000 in crypto income
chunks.text:
- In early 2021 Jack switched from general YouTube videos to crypto videos. His third video hit 60,000 views and his fourth 120,000, while his top video on the old channel had about 12,000.
- The new channel earned over $3,000 in YouTube ad revenue in its first month.
- He describes the crypto audience as a niche "no one is serving," and he was "the only one really making videos around it."
- He loved the topic at first, and that enthusiasm helped him post daily.

chunks.heading: How the $500,000 was made: an NFT project plus a mining add-on
chunks.text:
- In summer 2021 he launched an NFT project of stick figures he drew himself.
- He hired a developer on a 40% commission.
- He added a mining operation on top, which netted about $700 to $1,000 every five days, boosted by his YouTube channel.
- The NFT collection (6,969 items) sold out in a week.
- Combined net revenue came to roughly $500,000, paid entirely in cryptocurrency.
- The plan behind it was to make daily videos and build something to sell to his audience. That way he could control his own time and income on the internet, which is why he had dropped out of college and quit McDonald's.

chunks.heading: The tax mistake: crypto income is taxed at the price received
chunks.text:
- Income paid in crypto is taxed at its value when received, not at its value when the tax bill arrives.
- He did not understand this. He held all his crypto and sold none of it, even as prices fell.
- When the tax bill and accountant invoice arrived, the total was $31,000.
- The crypto he had earned was by then worth only about $70,000.
- He sold 70% of his crypto just to pay the accountant and the taxes, which took his entire net profit for roughly a year and a half.
- He was left with about $30,000 of profit, mostly from the mining proceeds, because the NFT sales "evaporated completely."
- His lesson in effect: when income is paid in a volatile asset, set aside cash for the tax bill at the time you receive it.

chunks.heading: Spending mistakes and admin friction
chunks.text:
- He paid his developer about CAD $200,000.
- He then hired other people to work on the project. They either did not move the needle or delivered subpar work, so he "was losing money fast" paying for work that made no progress.
- His accountant dropped him because she was scared to file his crypto taxes.
- His replacement was a crypto specialist who put "crypto" in the corporate name. As a result he could not get a business bank account.
- Fixing it meant switching accountants and paying about $700 to change the corporation name.

chunks.heading: Burnout and the pivot away from crypto
chunks.text:
- The loss sat in his stomach for a month. He "didn't want to get out of bed" and felt like an idiot for having "the easiest goal wealth" and still fluffing it.
- Months of daily videos on the same topic drained his spark. He realized he did not want to talk about crypto all day for the rest of his life, because the topic "just not something that grabs me."
- He started a blog and newsletter called The Freaking Philosophy, about lessons and failures, aimed at building a philosophy for a better life.
- He moved his YouTube channel to the new topic and cut off the 25,000-subscriber crypto channel.
- He accepts that he lost thousands of subscribers and business learning potential, and says he does not care.
- He writes the newsletter for many hours a day, and is also working on a book.

chunks.heading: Principles he takes away
chunks.text:
- "Easy money will elude you just like it did me, so don't go for easy, go for doing something you actually want to do for the rest of your life."
- He says what you are doing, who you are with and where you are matter more than how much money you make or lose. Money matters less in the long run than fulfillment.
- He used to think success was about hustling and making money. Now he thinks it is about finding your "good work," meaning work you can do really well, and making that work.
- He ties his choice of topic to sustainability: a niche can grow fast, but if you do not enjoy it you cannot keep making content about it for years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack reflects on hitting about $50/day from an app with premium features, and why that small number buys autonomy and keeps him out of a job. He argues for owning a scalable product, helping people genuinely, and treating paying users as real validation.

chunks.heading: Why Jack aims for about $50/day online instead of a job
chunks.text:
- In October 2024 Jack had made about $50 a day for roughly a month and a half from an app he built. He says he is not selling T-shirts or dropshipping from Alibaba. He is "actually helping people."
- He treats $50/day as a milestone because it lets him avoid employment. He is not saying everyone should skip jobs. It is what he wants for his own life.
- His main reasons are time freedom and autonomy.
- He says "I would much rather have my own business, my own company than work for somebody else."
- He had planned to get a job in the six months before this video. About a month earlier his app was not making money, and then he had "a turning point."

chunks.heading: The math of $50/day and living cheaply
chunks.text:
- $50/day is about $1,500 a month. He says it is still close to $1,500 after tax, because his government would not tax someone earning under roughly $16,000 a year.
- He lives near Toronto, Canada, and says he spends very little. He lives with his mother and pays about $600 in rent.
- He admits living on under about $16,000 a year is not very sustainable for most people. He says he is lucky to be in this position.
- He sees low expenses as what makes a small income enough to keep him independent. In his words, $50 a day "can keep employment away."

chunks.heading: Scalable leverage: why $50/day and $500/day take similar effort
chunks.text:
- Jack says that from his side, going from $50/day to $500/day (or $5,000) takes about the same effort. The difference is more people coming to his website or app.
- A user pressing the buy button costs him almost nothing. He pays only small backend costs and some credits.
- He built the app once. People pay for its premium features or to remove ads, and he does not have to rebuild it for each sale.
- He argues that having no need for employment now can turn into having no need for employment later, because the same product can scale.
- He does not claim the income is easy. He says it is "hard but really fun."

chunks.heading: Paying customers are the validation that matters
chunks.text:
- Jack says payment from users is worth far more than kind comments. "People paying me for my product... is immensely more valuable than people just commenting saying like oh that's cool."
- Paying users show the product is liked and is helping them. They also contact him to say so.
- He uses a hypothetical to make the point. If 10,000 people downloaded the app and nobody paid for premium features, that would be "okay" and have room to grow, but it would not be real validation.
- He says payment validation is what supports a "keep going mentality." It tells him the business could actually work.

chunks.heading: Value creation and ownership as the basis for a business
chunks.text:
- He says helping people is "the only way to have a successful business." He calls anything else "a fugazi" or a scam, and says "something scummy."
- His goal is to "provide value and get paid for the value that I provide," and to deliver more value than people pay for. He calls this the main goal: "overdeliver."
- He prefers owning the business because the cause and effect is firsthand. Any upside comes back to him in full. If he made $10,000 on a good day, he would be paid the whole $10,000 and not a bonus.
- He feels he can make more of a difference this way than by working for someone else.

chunks.heading: Building in public and following what he wants
chunks.text:
- Jack documents the process on his channel as raw as possible. He says that is the whole point of the channel. He also made this video as a record for his future self.
- His public mission is to end doomscrolling, through his app that helps with doomscrolling. He is also writing a book called "consumption control."
- He studied computer programming for two and a half years and got very good grades. He did not want to work eight hours a day at a desk for someone else.
- He now works more than 8 hours a day, but on his own projects. He says there is an "unlimited ceiling" when he builds something of his own, and a "very limited ceiling" when he works by the hour.
- He says he has less "bottled up anxiety" when he follows what he actually wants from life. He says he has spent a lot of time asking himself what that is, and is not only going with his gut.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A one-year progress update on building Curiosity Quench, an app that replaces doomscrolling with activities matched to people's curiosity. Jack walks through the timeline from a no-code web prototype and viral clips to 95K downloads and $30K revenue, with half of that revenue landing in the last two months.

chunks.heading: Curiosity Quench: what the app does and the core idea behind it
chunks.text:
- Jack's app, "Curiosity Quench", is meant to end doomscrolling. At day 365 he was still building it alone.
- Its goal is not to block or restrict anything. It helps people find things they would enjoy more than scrolling their phone.
- His thesis is that curiosity is the cure for boredom, and "you can't stop" curiosity. He applies this to the social media era this way: find a topic you care about and try it.
- The flow:
  1. Browse more than 1,000 topics and swipe right to save one to a list.
  2. Get a plan to try the topic.
  3. Each step in the plan links to curated content that helps you do it.
  4. Finish the plan and "quench" the curiosity.
- He built it because he believes most people scrolling TikTok have a lot of potential. He wants them to act on their real curiosity instead of feeding dopamine loops. He also built it for himself.

chunks.heading: Building in public: a daily video log for 365 days
chunks.text:
- Jack started by documenting the build on TikTok. His first video said he was building an app "to destroy TikTok", meaning the addiction to it and not TikTok itself.
- He then made 365 daily videos. About 360 of them are daily YouTube logs, which are longer and go deeper on what he is doing.
- In the first month he had nothing to show and only talked about the idea. Many people reacted well, especially on TikTok, with comments like "this is a great idea." That feedback is why he went ahead and built it.
- His advice is that 365 days "isn't a long time" and passes quickly if you commit every day. He has enjoyed the logs and will keep making them for now.

chunks.heading: From no-code web app to a mobile app
chunks.text:
- He didn't know how to code when he started. His early attempt to code it himself was "a mess" and he gave up quickly.
- He made a no-code prototype by about day 10.
- He launched the no-code web version around December, roughly 60 days in.
- The first version was primitive and made no money. He says it wasn't very good and didn't help people much.
- The web app was the only version for the first four months or so.
- The mobile app was released in February, about 4 to 5 months after he started.
- Early web users gave the mobile app a starting base of users.
- Over the year he learned to code and to design. He says he is "not a professional by any means."
- He got design help from a freelancer he credits as "Cats". She did a redesign that changed the look a lot.
- He removed the ugly banner ads and the "claim credits" ads that he had put everywhere.

chunks.heading: Validation signals that kept him going
chunks.text:
- A reel showing the web app got 400K views at around day 60. He said he didn't expect it.
- He later refers to 300K real views of him showing "a really bad web app."
- He took that as proof of interest: "I'm sure there's something here." The traction is what made him start coding the web version for real.
- Installs on the mobile app reached 95,000. About a month before the video it was only about 50,000, so a lot happened at once.
- After launch there was roughly three months of little progress, especially on revenue. The app wasn't making money and wasn't sustainable at that point.
- He could have quit then but didn't. The reminder he pasted everywhere was "KEEP GOING" in all caps, which he says was really all it took at that stage. He adds that it obviously took much more than that.

chunks.heading: Results at 1 year and the 80/20 pattern in revenue
chunks.text:
- The app has made more than $30K so far. He calls that "pretty good."
- About half of that, roughly $15K, came in the last two months. He didn't state the dollar figure, so this is derived from "half of $30K".
- In his words, two of the 12 months gave 50% of the results. He cites it as an example of the Pareto principle, the 80/20 rule.
- The lesson is that results can come late and in a lump. Most of the year had low results, and he kept going anyway.
- At the time he was running a sale: 40% off annual plans and 30% off monthly plans.

chunks.heading: Why marketing became the priority over product
chunks.text:
- Recently he wasn't working on the app itself. Marketing was the priority.
- His reasoning is that you can only make the app so good. You can always improve it, and he wants to, but if he doesn't tell people about it, nobody downloads it and nobody sees the better parts.
- At this stage, distribution mattered more than more product polish.
- He still keeps the product sharp. The site now has a clear mission, a clear goal and many testimonials, which it lacked at the start.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack live-streams vibe coding his mobile food diary app (Doof) in React Native/Expo using Cursor. He shows how he prompts AI to fix bugs, picks models that stay on task, and designs a coin-flip feature to stop cravings. He also shares his plan for organic-only marketing and a hard paywall.

chunks.heading: Building Doof with AI-assisted "vibe coding" in React Native and Expo
chunks.text:
- Jack builds Doof, a food diary app for tracking what you eat and how it makes you feel. He built it for himself after noticing chocolate gave him headaches. The App Store name is "food diary to quit junk", which fits the 30-character limit exactly.
- The stack is React Native and Expo. Jack made a boilerplate and shares it through his Discord. Data lives in a local Expo SQLite database, so the app works fully offline with no server.
- He does almost no hand-coding on this app. He says: "I'm not doing any coding today it's called Vibe coding we are just asking cursor what to do and then it does it."
- Fast Refresh shows JavaScript changes in the simulator immediately. Installing a package needs a rebuild of about a minute.
- He ran this as a live stream, "day 3" of a 30-day build. He skipped the day 2 video because he was lazy, and says he got more done by not worrying about it.
- He wants to track his own food and feelings, then use that history to decide what to eat next.

chunks.heading: Working with Cursor and AI models effectively
chunks.text:
- **Model choice:** Jack uses Claude 3.5 inside Cursor for most work. Claude 3.7 "adds so much data" and extra features he didn't ask for, even with Cursor rules telling it not to.
- **Database risk:** 3.7 helped build the initial database. It later "took some initiative and it broke and it dropped my table" with data in it. He now has import/export, so he can export data before risky changes.
- **Docs-driven setup:** For Expo SQLite he pasted the documentation into Cursor, and also copy-pasted the whole page, because "it usually doesn't read the links I send." It worked in about two tries. The first errors went back into the chat and it fixed them.
- **How to copy docs:** Highlight only the documentation content, from the top header to the bottom, and skip the rest of the page.
- **Be specific when it fails:** Cursor repeatedly failed to show a saved "was this a craving" value. The cause was a data-type mismatch: the database stores a Boolean as 0/1 and it wasn't converted back. Jack fixed it by telling Cursor exactly what to do.
- **Accept or reject per change:** He often rejects unwanted additions, such as an extra delete button, and re-prompts with a narrower instruction ("I just want the answer if any to be toggled in the edit... don't change card data").
- **Stuck sessions:** When Cursor stalled, he stopped it, restarted the app, and opened a fresh composer or chat session.
- **Tailwind:** He doesn't use it for React Native and sticks to default styles. He says simple styling goes a long way.

chunks.heading: Advice for beginners starting their first app
chunks.text:
- If you have no development experience, describe your idea to ChatGPT, bolt.new or v0. Jack calls v0 and bolt.new the best bets.
- Follow what the tool tells you, get something up and out there, and learn as you go.
- Expect to read a lot of documentation and make mistakes. He says "that's like the only way to really get through that is to learn and if you're interested enough you will go through that."
- His own first app took months, so he tells beginners not to get discouraged.
- **Simulators:** An iOS simulator needs a Mac with Xcode. Without a Mac, use the Android simulator, which "kind of sucks" but works. Jack built his first app on it.
- **Physical phone:** Some features can't be tested on a simulator, such as on-device ML, so some people test on a real phone.
- **Expo Go:** It is very limited. You can't use custom SDKs such as Superwall or RevenueCat, "pretty much the things you're going to need."

chunks.heading: Designing the coin-flip "chance" feature to curb temptation
chunks.text:
- **Purpose:** The feature adds a last layer of friction before eating something you shouldn't. Jack wanted to flip a coin to decide whether to eat a chocolate bar, but never has a coin on him. His paywall already advertises a "flip a coin" feature.
- **Iterating with the AI:** The first Cursor version worked but was clunky, with flipped check marks and always saying "go for it." Jack asked for "more dramatic," a bigger coin and a cleaner, lighter UI.
- **Assets:** He first tried custom Figma coin images (check, X, blank), then switched to emojis, which "feel like not serious" and looked better than the AI-looking version. He wants proper heads/tails coin icons later and found free animated flip-coin graphics on Rive.
- **Final mechanic:**
  1. The user types what they're tempted to eat.
  2. They call heads or tails (heads by default).
  3. They flip the coin.
  4. If they call it right, they can eat it. If wrong, they skip it.
- **Why 50/50:** He dropped odds adjustment, such as a 20% chance, to keep it simple. Earlier he had considered a max of 50%.
- **Cooldown:** He chose a 30-second cooldown (first thought was once per hour). The input is disabled after flipping, so users can't change their call. Users can still ignore the result, so it's one last nudge, not enforcement.
- **UI polish:** The flip button sits sticky at the bottom, with result info above it. He plans to auto-fill the food name from where the user taps in, and to prompt users to log the food after a "yes."
- **Priorities:** He says the coin flip "doesn't have to be that great" and should stay clean and a bit fun. He chose it over the filtering system because it's "more fun to watch."

chunks.heading: Product principles for the food log and dashboard
chunks.text:
- **Core value:** The app isn't meant to say what's healthy. It's for logging how your body reacted so you can decide with more information next time. People forget how bad something felt, so a note like "do not eat this again" sways later decisions.
- **Log fields:** Food name, how much you liked it, whether it was worth it, whether it was a craving, notes, hunger, digestive comfort, sleep quality, mental clarity, time eaten and location. A daily reminder is time-selectable and can be turned off.
- **Names over photos:** He rejected photo-based auto-categorizing. It's a lot of work, and he wants to type the name he'll remember. A photo of his chicken stew labeled "chicken stew" wouldn't match how he'd search for it. Search already covers notes.
- **Rating scale:** He tried sliders and 1-10 and didn't like them, so he kept 1-7. He chose 7 because 6 has no middle.
- **Dashboard plan:** The current dashboard is "terrible" and will be redone. He wants it to show:
  - which foods most often make the person feel good
  - which foods they should avoid
  - suggestions like "when you eat fruits in the morning you have a much better mood"
- **Local AI idea:** An offline local model could generate insights at zero cost. He notes many Android users have older devices that may not run one well.
- **Notifications:** After onboarding, a popup explains daily reminders. If the user denies permission, small text points them to device settings to enable it.

chunks.heading: Monetization, launch and distribution plan for Doof
chunks.text:
- **Hard paywall:** After onboarding and personalized insights, users hit a paywall. They can exit but can't use the core features without paying. Jack says: "I have made free stuff before and... no one pays so trying to be profitable business here."
- **Marketing:** He'll market Doof fully organically through social, with no ad spend at first, and maybe hire influencers later. He'll use his own app, Post Bridge, for posting. He hasn't yet worked out what the videos will be about.
- **Branding:** A friend, Desmond, noted that an emoji-style logo, like the coconut emoji in the app "Coconote," can build familiarity and trust. Jack compared his own watermelon logo with a banana emoji and kept his green watermelon logo, noting the icon looks better zoomed out.
- **Store submission:** He plans to also publish on Google Play, calling it about an hour of extra work. Google Play needs a closed-testing release before production for new developer accounts, which he found annoying and may skip.
- **Working style:** Streaming is a build-in-public channel. He admits he doesn't know how full-day streamers do it, and notes it's "its own game" apart from building a business.
- **Time split:** He also runs his SaaS (Post Bridge), so he streams for short stretches and then goes back to other work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack explains his organic social playbook for B2C apps, drawn from getting his earlier app to 100k downloads. Warm up a fresh account by scrolling only in-niche content, post manually and slowly, recreate proven viral formats as value-first content (never ads), and convert through comments.

chunks.heading: Warming up a new account before posting (Jack's B2C app playbook)
chunks.text:
Jack's plan for getting 1,000 downloads to a B2C app for $0 is organic Instagram and TikTok content. He says about 95% of his results came from Instagram. His earlier app, Curiosity Quench, reached 100,000 downloads across three accounts that used the same format.

- **Use a brand new account.** Don't reuse an old one. An old account carries its past interests, and the algorithm keeps pushing content to that old audience, which is "very hard" to change. Zero followers is fine. A single video with 200k views will bring followers.
- **Don't post for the first 2-3 days.** Jack prefers 3 days or more. He says: "if your account is not warm it doesn't matter how good your content is it will not get reach." Skipping this step is why most people get under 300 views per video.
- **Use the account like a human for 15 minutes a day.** Jack sets an actual timer. Do this per account and per platform.
- **Engage only with videos in your niche.** Skip everything else. Watch videos to the end, comment, and follow niche accounts. Don't mass-like or mass-comment, because that looks like a bot.
- **Search for your niche to shape the feed.** The For You page won't match your app at first. Jack searched "healthy foods" for his food-diary app and followed niche accounts. After about 10-15 interactions the feed fills with relevant content.
- **Warm up on your phone.** Jack believes TikTok in particular trusts mobile devices more, because a real device is harder to spoof than web.
- **Save ideas while you scroll.** After 2-3 days you should have roughly 10-30 videos to recreate for your app.
- **Use one account at a time per phone.** Jack tried warming two at once and got no reach. If he ran six accounts, he'd use a VPN or separate phones.

chunks.heading: Posting cadence and manual posting for new accounts
chunks.text:
Jack treats the first week of posting as a period for looking human to the algorithm.

- **Post the first ~7 videos manually, from your phone.** Scheduling tools post through an API, and "bots post things through the API, humans don't." Move the file to your phone and upload it in the app.
- **Post one video per day for the first week.** Two on some days is acceptable. His maximum ever was about 3 a day to one account, on Instagram.
- **If you post more than once a day, space posts 3-4 hours apart.** Don't post "seven reels within 1 hour" or one every 10 minutes. His view of TikTok is that it "hates when you spam videos like every 10 minutes."
- **Reply to comments.** This builds presence on a new account.
- **Start slow and raise volume gradually.** Spamming usually leaves a new account with fewer than 200 views per video. If an account's videos already get 5,000+ views each, more frequent posting (still 2-4 hours apart) may be fine.
- **Switch to a scheduler after the first week.** Jack plans to schedule through Post Bridge, the tool he built. Afterward he only opens the apps to reply to comments.
- **Add a second account only once the first is working.** His rule is to wait until the first account gets thousands of views a day. Otherwise, post more often to one warm account.
- **A bad start is normal.** If the first 10 videos get only 10-100 views, stick to the plan. Stop posting for 2 days, keep warming up, and take it slowly.
- **Expect a few thousand views from one video within about two weeks.** If none reaches that, slow down.
- **Multiple platforms:** Post the same videos to TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Twitter/X threads and Facebook. Pinterest also needs warming up. Jack added Pinterest to Post Bridge but never warmed it up, and he gets zero views there.

chunks.heading: Finding viral video formats and recreating them
chunks.text:
Jack doesn't invent formats from scratch. He finds videos that already work in his niche and recreates them for his app.

- **Source of ideas:** the warmed-up For You page. For his food-diary app Doof, he found photo carousels of healthy meals with tens of thousands of likes. One had 82,000 likes, and another had 26,000.
- **Recreate the pattern.** For Doof, that means a photo carousel of food with a POV caption and trendy audio. The last slide shows the app logging the food, how it made him feel, and notes.
- **Use any source of images.** AI-generated images, internet images, Pinterest, or your own photos all work.
- **Adapt formats across niches.** Jack's example is an informational photo post for a habit tracker, such as "how to build healthy habits that last long."
- **Make it valuable first.** The value can be a laugh, making viewers feel seen, teaching them something, or giving them recipes.
- **Don't be the only judge.** Jack says "not everyone is you," so something you find boring may do well. Post it, iterate, and improve each video a little.
- **Tools:** CapCut (free, runs on desktop or phone, about a day to learn), Post Bridge, and each platform's native editor. Jack made videos in TikTok's native editor for his first 4-5 months.
- **Hooks:** Jack has no special prompting strategy. He makes apps for himself and makes the videos he would find funny or interesting. Daily posting lets you test different hooks.

chunks.heading: Never make an ad: value content with a comment-section call to action
chunks.text:
Jack's main rule for organic app marketing is that a video must not look like an ad.

- "Never make an ad. Ads do not perform, they don't go viral." Straight ads get pushed down to about 200 views. If you're making an ad, he says, "might as well just spend money on ads."
- **Sell solutions and results.** Don't put the product in front of people's faces.
- **Product demos:** A demo longer than about 5 seconds is probably an ad, and viewers skip ads about 90% of the time. Standalone product demos typically get under 1,000 views. Demos can work as a short clip at the end (about 5 seconds, "download this") over background footage of someone using the app.
- **Better approach:** Show screenshots or bits of the app's UI inside valuable content. Viewers then ask in the comments "what app is this?" and visit the app page.
- **Call to action:** Comment on the video, pin the comment, and put the download link in the caption. Jack calls this "the best way to do it."
- **First videos:** You don't need an app call to action in them. Get some traction first.
- **Why this works:** Jack says most conversions come from the comment section. A video with 3 million views converts even if only a small share of viewers download.

chunks.heading: Formats Jack has used and the results
chunks.text:
- **"2x2 fade" hobby format for Curiosity Quench.** Images of hobbies, text and a catchy sound. After about 200 of these videos, several got millions of views, including one at 600k. Once four in a row hit millions of views, Jack built the format into Post Bridge. The format works because viewers "feel seen" and fill the comments. It contains no product mention, only small pieces of the UI.
- **Talking to the camera about what he built that day.** Jack did this 360 times on his personal account. He posted the same kind of video 343 days in a row. Most got about 4K views, then one hit 1.3 million. Others reached 800k and still brought in downloads.
- **Habit Garden (his friend Mark's habit app).** Jack made a new account, warmed it up for 3 days, and posted 12 videos. The first videos got a few hundred views. After the fifth video he reused the 2x2 meme format from his other app, with memes, emojis and a controversial angle. One video got 5,000 views and the next got 5 million, which brought a few thousand visitors to the app. Other accounts then copied the videos.
- **Keep what works.** If a format still produces results, "milk the crap out of" it. A brand account doesn't need new formats while the old one works. Jack still uses the same format daily on his own apps.
- **Don't rely on a single format.** The 2x2 format is limited, and higher-converting formats exist.
- **Expect many misses.** Jack posted hundreds of videos (about 800 on one account) before seeing traction. One hit shows what works, and then you repeat it.
- **Platform notes:**
  - Instagram pushes content that resonates with an audience, regardless of geography. He has seen people in Asia do well with US audiences (example: the Rise app).
  - TikTok favors the US and Canada and is hit or miss for him.
  - Trendy audio helps because people like good-sounding music. Being on the official trending sound page isn't the reason.
  - US reach on TikTok: some people use a US account with a US SIM, or a US account with a VPN and Post Bridge, which has US servers.

chunks.heading: Doof launch and 30-day challenge plan
chunks.text:
- **Challenge:** Build an app in 30 days, then reach 1,000 users and $100 in revenue. This stream is day 8. The app was already live on the App Store.
- **Day-one results:** About 300 downloads and 23 trials started from a single tweet, with no other marketing.
- **What Doof is:** A food diary to quit junk food. It tracks how foods make you feel (digestion, sleep, temptation), not calories. Jack says logging is "10 to 100 times easier" than a calorie tracker.
- **Marketing split:** Jack says getting downloads is "90% of the game" of making money in the App Store. Once the app is built, he stops coding and spends his time on marketing.
- **Plan:**
  - Warm up TikTok and Instagram accounts on his phone.
  - Save 10-30 ideas.
  - Post reels first to build discovery and followers.
  - Add photo carousels later, which he says have been performing well and are easy to make.
- **Why one viral video matters:** A video with 1,000 or 100,000 downloads also boosts the app's natural App Store ranking.
- **Who it works for:** Wide-appeal B2C apps (health and wellness suit TikTok and Instagram). He says it doesn't work easily for B2B.
- **Niche apps:** For a narrow audience like a YouTube organizer, memes won't work. Jack suggests higher prices, paid ads, or face-to-camera videos that explain the tool, and says it's harder.
- **Finance and similar categories:** These may need LinkedIn or Reddit, which is a different strategy. Jack hasn't marketed an app there.

chunks.heading: Paywall, onboarding and tech stack for Doof
chunks.text:
- **Paywall:** Doof has a hard paywall with no freemium. Jack says a hard paywall "is just going to make more money." He uses freemium on some other apps. If a business is chasing a revenue goal, he goes hard paywall and may free up features later.
- **Onboarding:** Extensive, at least about 10 pages, if the app blocks users behind a paywall. The onboarding has to explain why the app will help them, or they delete it.
- **Free logging before the paywall:** Users can skip the first paywall and log one food. They see how logging works, their dashboard, streak, food mood and recommended foods. The hard paywall appears when they try to log a second food.
- **Stack:** React Native with Expo, Cursor, and sometimes Supabase for the backend. He uses a boilerplate with payments and onboarding already set up, linked in his Discord.
- **Scale:** He built with scale in mind. Hosting cost a few more dollars as usage grew.
- **Learning to build:** For people new to coding, Jack suggests cloning the boilerplate into Cursor, reading the Expo docs, and pasting every error into ChatGPT.
- **Post Bridge:** A scheduler Jack built to post to Instagram, TikTok, Twitter and Facebook at once. It has no API yet, but one is in the works. He has used it for every Curiosity Quench post for four months, and the posts weren't shadow-banned because the accounts were warm.
- **Paid creators:** Jack has little experience. He prefers hiring creators to post on branded accounts, such as "app number two", instead of on the creator's own account. He has messaged creators from his personal account.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack live-streams revamping the onboarding of his food-mood app Doof after weak trial conversions. He moves to a hard, non-dismissible paywall, lengthens onboarding with personalization and feature carousels, and uses Figma mockups fed to Cursor to build it. He studies competitor onboardings and iterates copy many times.

chunks.heading: Why Jack is rebuilding his app's onboarding and making the paywall a hard gate
chunks.text:
- Jack's food-mood app "Doof" was live on the App Store, but its onboarding was weak. It had 3 sell-the-problem screens, 5 questions, a loading animation, tips, and then a paywall. That is about 9 interactions in total.
- A tweet pointed out that he had too little onboarding and a skippable paywall. He admits he "made a decent onboarding" but has "no great system to capture people who are downloading my app and make sure that they are ready to buy by the time that the paywall comes up."
- Status at the time:
  - Almost 400 downloads in total.
  - 62 new users.
  - No revenue yet.
  - 26 trial starts in the last 7 days, and most were cancelled right away.
  - Zero conversions in the last 24 hours.
- He had already removed free trials. His reasoning: get the true conversion rate of the onboarding first, then A/B test trials. A 7-day trial delays the conversion signal.
- His trial view: 3-day trials are okay, but 7-day trials have worked better on his other apps (including Curiosity Quench). He plans to add a trial back and test it after the onboarding converts.

chunks.heading: Hard paywall setup with Superwall
chunks.text:
- Jack removed the X and the "skip" paths. After onboarding, 100% of users see a gated paywall they cannot pass without paying. The coin-flip feature and the second food log also trigger gated paywalls.
- Discount flow: users cannot dismiss the paywall. If they start a purchase and cancel it, they get another discount offer. The discount element sits at the bottom of the paywall.
- Apple approves hard paywalls. His rule: put a disclaimer in the app description and "make it abundantly clear that there is paid content." Apple approved his paywall and the app.
- Superwall campaigns use triggers placed in the app, such as a "flip coin" trigger. You can:
  - Remove the paywall entirely.
  - Show it to only 50% of users.
  - Show different paywalls to different groups and compare results.
- Paywalls and gating can change over the air with no app update.
- He picked Superwall over RevenueCat because RevenueCat has very limited paywall functionality. He used both together on Curiosity Quench, but on a fresh start he uses Superwall only.
- He built the paywall from a Superwall template in about 1 to 1.5 hours, adding his own copy, logo, and products.
- For plan tests (for example quarterly vs yearly, or yearly vs monthly), split traffic 50/50 and run it for 1 to 2 months. Keep whichever makes more money. He says Superwall makes this easy.
- Setting up Superwall and RevenueCat took him 2 to 3 weeks the first time.
- His stack: React Native, Expo, and Superwall, with no login. Data is local only, which saves him auth work.

chunks.heading: Why longer onboarding helps conversion
chunks.text:
- Jack's reasoning: a longer flow is a time investment. By the paywall, users have already put in a cost, so they are more likely to pay.
- Questions about goals help for two reasons. People who state a goal are more serious about it, and the app can affirm them for it.
- A fake "calculating" stage after the questions makes the result feel more tailored and valuable, even though the result is ready instantly. He calls it an easy way to raise perceived value.
- Benchmarks from his research: he screenshotted every screen of competitor apps by downloading them (he skipped Mobbin as too costly):
  - Slide counts of 43, 36, 177, and about 8.
  - Death Clock asks about 25 questions. Much of that is time investment, plus a shareable result.
  - Quitter has about 40 slides, goal setting, and carousels. It uses a hard paywall with no trial, only yearly or monthly.
- His target is to roughly double his flow (about 9 to about 18 steps). He says 177 slides "works but it is crazy."
- He says his own taste leans toward showing how the app helps before asking for money. A flow that only says "here's your problem" and then asks for payment loses him. Part of why he wants this change is that the old flow never showed how the app solves the problem.
- Key principle: "a lot of how effective this app is going to be to help people is based in the onboarding. Do they believe it's going to work... can they see how it directly impacts their life."

chunks.heading: The new Doof onboarding flow
chunks.text:
1. Welcome splash with a get-started button. Copy: "find the foods that fuel your body best." Lowercase, matching the app's playful name. Below it, a note that no login is required and the user's data is 100% theirs.
2. Name input. Stored locally. Jack notes some apps ask for a name and never use it. It still eases the user in.
3. Goal selection with about four preset goals and a custom entry.
4. A congratulations screen. Draft copy: "Cheers to you."
5. A feature carousel with 8 screens, using his App Store screenshots. Each has a title and subtitle:
   - Log food: "log once, learn forever."
   - Track how your food makes you feel.
   - A history screen: "your personal food memory bank" and "see your history, change your future."
   - A dashboard of food moods and streaks: "your food mood patterns tell a story."
   - The coin flip: "tempted by junk? let the coin decide your fate." Subtitle: stack the odds in your favor.
   - Recommendations from past logs: "log the good, get more good." These come purely from the user's own past logs, with no AI.
   - Whole-body impact and hidden food patterns.
   - Filter which foods fuel you and which drain you.
6. A "ready to find your fuel" screen: answer questions in 30 seconds to get personal insights.
7. A privacy-first screen: users own their data, and can export and import it.
8. The existing mood/energy questions, the insights, and then the hard paywall.

- Jack also planned to ask for an app rating in the flow.
- The screenshots were reused from the App Store listing because he had already spent time on that copy. He reuses them as proof of what the app does.
- Onboarding messaging should match App Store positioning. People download for specific reasons: track how food feels, avoid repeating mistakes, and find foods that fuel them best.

chunks.heading: Copywriting and design workflow
chunks.text:
- Copy takes iteration. Jack spent about 1.5 hours with ChatGPT and his own brain on the headings, and made about 10 versions of each slide. He says "you're going to have to iterate through like 10 different versions."
- He asks Cursor for subheading ideas because it has his project context. He gives it the title and the screenshot, then picks the best of the options.
- His mockup process:
  - He builds a very rough layout in Figma, using the competitor screenshots as references.
  - He feeds the mockup and screenshots to Cursor, then tweaks by hand where Cursor fails.
  - He says it is "mockup time, not design time," and that he is a Figma beginner.
- Cursor tips from the session:
  - Tell it exactly what to change and to touch nothing else. Otherwise it rewrites unrelated screens.
  - Give it good references and keep prompting for small changes, adjusting with your own taste.
  - He had issues with Claude 3.7 doing things he did not ask for. He considered switching to 3.5.
  - The first Cursor attempt looked awful, so he rejected it and gave a reference image instead.
- Technical details he asked Cursor for:
  - Bottom buttons in the same position on every slide.
  - Lowercase copy.
  - A fix for the keyboard covering the inputs.
  - Auto-capitalization turned off.
  - A vertical-offset variable per slide image.
- The change requires an app update, so he planned to push it to the App Store and start marketing the next day.

chunks.heading: Marketing and launch advice Jack gave
chunks.text:
- He is building the app as part of a 30-day challenge (day 9). The point is to show how easy it is to market a project, and that marketing matters more than the app itself.
- Organic short-form video on TikTok and Instagram is his go-to channel for getting free users. Watch what performs on each platform, make similar videos, and reuse them across both.
- Competing apps do not rely only on paid ads; they have organic content that performs. Content must be valuable, not ads.
- Launch early: "if it's crap you can just fix it later." Waiting risks burnout or never launching.
- For a Play Store requirement of 12 testers, he suggests a TikTok video asking for free testers, with a link in your bio to collect emails.
- Ideas: build something you will use yourself, and paste your idea into ChatGPT to ask how to build it as a web app.
- Getting started: open Cursor, Bolt, v0, or ChatGPT and start building, or follow a tutorial. He learned by building with ChatGPT and reading docs only when stuck, with no courses. He had been coding for about 1.5 years.
- He doubts "vibe coding" works for the long term without thinking, but says AI coding is not going away.
- Post Bridge: US-based accounts must be warmed up in the US before posting through it. A VPN can be used just to connect the account.
- Designer help: his Curiosity Quench screens were doodled by a freelance designer. For Doof, he used a Superwall template and his own work.
- Testing: he uses the Xcode iPhone simulator (requires a Mac), a TestFlight phone, and App Review as a bug catcher.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Day 11 of building a mobile app: Jack live-streams making a short TikTok/Instagram video to drive downloads. He finds a proven format by scrolling his niche, recreates it with free AI images and CapCut, adds a call to action in the caption and pinned comment, and tests new formats daily.

chunks.heading: Warming up a new TikTok/Instagram account before posting
chunks.text:
- Jack's rule for a brand-new account: no posting for the first two days. He scrolls his niche for 15 to 50 minutes a day, and likes, comments on and follows accounts in that niche.
- The goal is for the algorithm to learn the niche, so the For You page feeds that niche back.
- For his food diary app account, he saved many videos from this scrolling to recreate later.
- If an account has already posted and gets under 100 views, he says to stop posting for a few days, scroll the niche, and then post once a day.
- If posting several times a day, space posts a few hours apart at minimum.
- If the For You page still isn't showing the niche, he suggests making a new account.
- On shadow banning: "Shadow Banning is kind of a thing but it's more or less if you're not acting like a human you're going to get less reach so act like a human."
- He says to use the platform for the first week so it treats you as a genuine user, then start posting.
- He says views can also depend on location. He is based in the US or Canada, and posting from elsewhere might change results.

chunks.heading: Finding formats to recreate instead of inventing content
chunks.text:
- Jack's process: find a format that has already done well, recreate it, post every day, and try different formats until one beats the others. Then reuse that format and repeat.
- He says to "try new formats", not "the same video over and over again" while hoping one goes viral.
- Source of ideas: videos he saved while warming up the account.
- Examples he reviewed in his niche:
  - A video with AI food pictures, which turned out to be an ad for a TikTok Shop.
  - A single grocery cart photo of healthy items with 655,000 likes, which he calls very easy to copy.
  - A video with the text "Society's normalized junk food so much that when someone eats real food it's considered dieting", over about 5 seconds of quick shots.
- He picked the third one: its message (junk food is normal, eating healthy gets called dieting) fits his app's theme of quitting junk food and eating healthy.
- He skipped a "no carbs" video because most of his content should be about quitting junk food and eating healthy.
- Expectations: "a lot of the time it takes like a week to get something that works." He expects a few weeks to land a good piece of content and work out the niche.
- He says a million views overnight can happen, but it's unlikely. Making more videos makes it more likely.

chunks.heading: Recreating a viral video in CapCut (live walkthrough)
chunks.text:
1. Get the original sound. Copy the video link, paste it into a TikTok downloader (he used Snaptik) and download it. If one downloader fails, try another. Watching an ad gets the HD version.
2. Drag the video into CapCut, put it on the track, and detach the audio.
3. Replace the visuals with his own images: put the original's text on top, then swap in his own pictures for the reference clips.
4. Count the images in the reference, since the pacing matters. His version was about 6 seconds with roughly 14 to 17 cuts, which he said is a good length per image.
5. Use the reference clip as a timing guide, then trim to match its length and delete the rest.
6. Raise the sound a bit and export.
7. Send the file to his phone and post natively.

- He says there are "a million ways" to do this, but this is how he does it and it works.
- Once he finds a format that works, he makes a CapCut template. He also mentions making them with code or with Postbridge.
- He sees the discovery stage as testing formats, not perfecting a template.
- Text: he tried several fonts and settled on Arial Bold for the default look.
- He tried a small shadow on the text, disliked it and reverted it.
- He argues the text being slightly hard to read can help, since it looks more natural. At about 6 seconds, people have to watch it two or three times before skipping, "which is exactly what we want."
- He checks the video on his phone before posting, since small text may not read on a desktop preview. It read fine on the phone.
- He adds small funny touches, such as a comment-style overlay. He says these can help a video spread without taking away from the message.

chunks.heading: Making free AI and stock images for videos (ImageFX)
chunks.text:
- Jack uses ImageFX, Google's free image tool, to generate the food photos.
- Prompts he used: "a plate of food top down", "healthy meal POV", "peeled mango", "healthy grocery cart POV", "healthy breakfast fruits", "healthy snack", "sweet potato mash dinner plate".
- He says POV prompts seem to work well. Portrait orientation (9:16) suits TikTok better.
- He sometimes grabs real photos from Google instead of AI.
- Quality rules:
  - Use varied foods. His first batch was the same thing over and over, so he swapped in different meals, snacks, a grocery shop and veggies.
  - Pick images that look like natural, real photos.
  - Reorder or replace weak images, and zoom in where an image needs it.
- On curation: "you do have to curate you can't just put out slop... doesn't get views for a good reason."
- He keeps a library of previously generated images in CapCut to reuse.

chunks.heading: Posting and call-to-action setup
chunks.text:
- Jack posts the same video to both TikTok and Instagram.
- He posts it natively from his phone with the original sound. He says you don't have to pick the official TikTok sound, as it usually recognizes it anyway.
- Caption:
  - He reuses the original's hashtags (food, diet, healthy, relatable, for you page).
  - He added a call to action with the app's search term, written like "quit junk for good using our app (food diary)", so people can search for it.
  - He also tried "find food that fuels you best", and says the call to action doesn't have to be perfect.
- When the video itself has no call to action, he makes the top comment one telling people to download the app. He copies the caption into a comment, adds a couple of emoji, and pins it on Instagram.
- He says if a video gets 1K views but no downloads, keep posting, keep trying new things, and make sure there's a call to action in the video, caption or comments. He also recommends a branded account.
- He didn't add a link in this post.
- After posting, he scrolls the home feed for about 5 seconds and interacts with similar videos. He watches them through, saves some, and comments. He says this isn't required.
- Targeting: his own followers (such as stream viewers) inflate views but aren't the target audience. An earlier video got 800 views mostly for that reason.
- If an account is in good standing, he keeps posting manually for now.

chunks.heading: Why content is the main driver of app downloads
chunks.text:
- Jack says getting people to download the app is "the biggest part of anything".
- On whether an app needs an Instagram or social account: "you really do need it... who's going to download your app if you don't talk about it". He says other approaches exist, but he thinks it's needed.
- He says "execution really is everything" now that apps are easier to build.
- Next content ideas for the food app:
  - A 4-image grid reel.
  - Recording himself as a user talking about the app, which he thinks would work well.
- Next product step: another iteration on onboarding, because the current version, though approved in review, "is still not that great".
- Context: this was day 11 of a 30-day challenge of building a viral mobile app, with free content as the distribution method. He says all the steps from the last few streams are in a guide he shared in the live chat.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack argues the simplest way to improve at or test any pursuit is to do it 100 times. Volume increases your odds of hitting something good, and you can stop early if you learn you don't like it. He applies it to his own 1,200 videos and book-writing.

chunks.heading: Doing something 100 times as the default way to get good
chunks.text:
- Jack's core advice: if you want to get better at something, or find out whether you want to do it at all, do it 100 times. He calls it simple, direct and unglamorous, and says simple advice is usually the most effective.
- The idea comes from Visakan Veerasamy ("visakanv") on Twitter. Jack applies it to his own work.
- Examples of the rule: to get better at public speaking, give 100 talks. To get better at talking to people, talk to 100 people.
- Jack calls it a numbers game. Do a hundred things and you either get better at it or some of them turn out good.
- He says almost nobody succeeds overnight. People know this but don't want to accept that the answer is just doing it 100, 1,000 or 100,000 times.

chunks.heading: Examples of volume producing quality
chunks.text:
- **Picasso:** he made about 50,000 pieces. Jack puts the ones that were true masterpieces at roughly 100, so under 1% were good enough to still matter today. The lesson is not to do fewer things. It is to do lots of things, keep trying and iterate.
- **Running:** a runner who keeps running improves, and one who stops doesn't. Jack says the choice of intervals, speed work or program matters less than continuing to run.
- **YouTube:** he mentions PewDiePie's reported advice to make 3,000 videos, not 300. Three videos give you low odds of a hit. 3,000 raise your odds and make you better at it.
- **Writing:** a great writer who "appears from nowhere" has usually written thousands of pieces before the one that hits.
- **Podcasting:** someone with 1,400 episodes (Joe Rogan is his example) is rarely in the bottom tier of hosts.
- **Music:** Kanye West said to lock yourself in a room and make five songs a day for three summers.
- **Ed Sheeran:** "when you turn on a dirty faucet, dirty water comes out for a long time. Then, eventually, clean water starts to flow." Jack's takeaway is that much of your output will be bad, but gems are buried in it, and doing many reps is how you find them. Even when it doesn't feel like progress, it is incremental progress.

chunks.heading: Applying reps to business and creative decisions
chunks.text:
- **Investor pitch:** build the deck 99 times and use the 100th version, since it is likely better than the 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 10th.
- **Starting a business:** sell 1,000 of something. His example is "shut up and sell 1,000 chocolate bars". He thinks the best advice for anything you want to create is to do it and repeat it many times.
- **Book title:** write around 400 possible titles and pick the best. The 400th is likely the product of iteration and refinement.
- Across all of these, quantity gives you more chances at quality and makes you better at the craft.

chunks.heading: You don't have to finish all 100
chunks.text:
- Jack says you don't need 100 reps of everything you start. Five, three or ten reps can be enough.
- His analogy is pizza pockets: you don't need to eat 100 to know whether you like them. Maybe you try six flavors and they're not for you, or maybe they are and you continue.
- The point is that you tried something and did something. Once you are doing things, the rest gets easier and falls into place, and you learn from it.
- Visakan's framing: drop the excuses and expectations, make 100 bad pieces with no reason and no agenda, at whatever pace feels comfortable. They can be bad or about things you don't care about. You will likely find something useful for your life.

chunks.heading: Progress shows up sooner than expected (the owl example)
chunks.text:
- Jack shows Visakan's owl drawings. Visakan set out to draw an owl 100 times, and by the 9th owl the drawing was noticeably better than the first three.
- Jack says the biggest barrier is expecting that you can't do enough reps to see progress. Nine reps was enough for a striking improvement.
- Each rep is a step forward, not always upward, because you move past what you did before.
- After nine owls you might be much better, or you might not have improved and keep going. Or you might decide you don't want to draw owls and stop, which is what Visakan did. You don't need the full 100 to learn what you need to know.

chunks.heading: Jack's own 100-rep projects
chunks.text:
- He had made about 1,200 YouTube videos over roughly two years earlier, then stopped making videos for a while.
- During the break he did a different set of reps: writing close to 100 chapters, about 100,000 words, and releasing a book. This video is a chapter from that unreleased book.
- This video is the first of a new run in which he plans to make 100 videos, likely daily.
- He also counts going to the gym and doing pull-ups as reps.
- He publishes the writing at freakit.net, with a weekly or twice-weekly newsletter, and says the book was released around the time of the video.
- His sign-off: stop watching videos and go do some things.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack argues that platforms profit from screen time over your lifetime, so regaining direction starts with knowing what you want out of life. His method is daily quiet time and boredom, which opens a "curiosity intake" that points you toward genuine interests you can pursue and act on.

chunks.heading: Why Jack says attention is the real problem to solve
chunks.text:
- Jack argues that attention is increasingly controlled by algorithms, mainly from social media but also other media that needs you present to make money.
- He says money is not the problem ("maybe the love of money is the bad part"). The problem is the incentive: many platforms, including YouTube, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook, are rewarded more for "screen time than lifetime".
- Result: there is more incentive to take up your lifespan and life force than to give it back.
- He treats attention as a commodity that these companies must treat as such to make money, and says engineers are "paid handsomely" to keep you on the screen.
- He frames this as the background for the app he was building at the time to curb doom scrolling (he said he had been working on it for "210 days", a figure that was garbled in the transcript, so treat it as approximate). He put the practical steps first and the app second.

chunks.heading: Step one: know what you want out of life
chunks.text:
- Jack says the key to escaping the cycle of being hooked back into attention-taking apps is knowing what you want out of life. The answer differs for each person.
- Once you know where you want to go, it is much easier to put the phone down and notice that "this thing in my hand is not getting me to where I want to go".
- It is not a one-time fix. Even when you know what you want, the other side of the screen is still engineered to keep you. He says "nothing is like that", meaning no single decision cures it.
- The answer can change, even daily, and that is fine. The goal is to find something you want, try to get it, stay interested and "make it enjoyable".
- He recommends asking yourself the question often, then giving yourself time to rest so your brain can think about it.

chunks.heading: Step two: do nothing and let your brain sort the clutter
chunks.text:
- Jack calls the first step counterintuitive: you do nothing. You sit and let your brain run wild, even though it will feel uncomfortable.
- His reasoning: years (he guesses 5 to 10) of scrolling have loaded the brain with a huge amount of information, which he compares to "hundreds of newspapers a day stacked over years". The brain has to sort through it.
- You must "get rid of the clutter" and clear your mind before you can find something you are interested in enough to build a life around.
- He avoids the label meditation, which he says has a bad rep, and calls it "quiet time".
- His own routine:
  - Every morning he sits down and is quiet.
  - He focuses on whatever is going on in his head, or on his breath.
  - He counts breaths from one to six (inhale one, exhale two, and so on), then restarts. He often loses count, and says that is fine.
- Alternatives that work the same way: going to the gym without music, or walking outside without music. He says the boring activities are therapeutic because they give real rest, not "I'm tired, I'll scroll".

chunks.heading: Boredom opens the "curiosity intake"
chunks.text:
- Jack's term: once you are bored enough, the "curiosity intake" opens. This is the intake for the things you are genuinely interested in and want to learn about.
- He says it is not a magic pill that hands you the answers. It gives you topics to question and dive into that come organically from your own head, not from an algorithm's feed.
- Why it matters: self-generated curiosity is a strong motivator to learn and take action.
- You work out what you want over time by introspecting on what you did and did not like, not by sitting still alone.
- The goal: scroll and use TikTok less, and be more inclined to follow your curiosity. He admits this sounds boring and that sitting with your eyes closed is "simple but not easy" if you are used to constant consumption.
- He notes that the content loop is weighted against human weaknesses, so the best individual defense is letting your brain genuinely rest and not overstimulating it too often.

chunks.heading: Find the primal emotion behind your goal
chunks.text:
- Jack believes most people want the same thing, which is to be happy.
- When you decide what you want, also decide why you want it. Ask what primal emotion it will bring: happiness, love, or perhaps fear (for example, fear that you won't get it, or fear of something else).
- Then focus on that primal emotion while doing the things that get you there. His claim is that the back of your head will then focus on what matters to you, not on the TikToks you just watched or the news around you.

chunks.heading: Jack's daily routine summary
chunks.text:
1. Allow yourself to be bored and under-stimulated, or at least not over-stimulated.
2. Take breaths. Make genuine rest a daily routine. It does not need to be meditation or sitting alone. A walk outside without music, or the gym without music, works.
3. Rest for about 10 minutes, then let the curiosity intake open.
4. Follow the things you are genuinely interested in and go down those rabbit holes as deeply as you can. He says what you want out of life is on the other side.
5. Keep asking yourself what you want, and leave time to rest so your brain can think about it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack explains how he built Postbridge, a simple social scheduler, for himself after expensive bloated tools frustrated him. He covers building in public as a journal, keeping a product lean, word-of-mouth through genuine value, and staying skeptical of AI in content and product.

chunks.heading: Why Jack builds for himself and keeps Post Bridge simple
chunks.text:
- Jack built Post Bridge in October 2024 for himself because every other social scheduler was "too expensive" and had "too much features."
- He made it "as simple as possible and as useful as possible for me." It turned out to be useful for others, which he did not expect in a red ocean market with many similar tools.
- He admits the approach does not solve everything: "you could make something that, you know, maybe only three other people want."
- His angle is value at a fair price. He does not argue "this is better, that's better." He points people to the pricing page and the features, because the tool does similar things and works.
- Because he uses the tool daily, he is incentivized to improve it for one specific customer. Right now that customer is mobile app founders.
- He does not compete on small things. He gives something of value, and people share it with friends. He says word of mouth has never gone as far for him as it has here.

chunks.heading: How he uses Post Bridge to market a mobile app
chunks.text:
- His app Curiosity Quench had about 60,000 downloads, many from organic videos.
- He makes a roughly six-second video and posts it to Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Twitter threads, Bluesky and more. Posting manually everywhere means uploading the same video each time. Post Bridge saves him ten to twenty minutes per video per day.
- After finding a video format that worked well, he automated it. In Post Bridge he fills in a simple template and it outputs the video. He does this daily and uploads to all channels from the app, running it close to autopilot ("not exactly autopilot").
- He also uses it for text posts. A tweet goes to Twitter, Threads, Facebook, LinkedIn and Bluesky, even though he only opens Twitter himself.
- His pinned tweet is a free guide to how he grew his mobile app with organic content. It is one of his most popular tweets because it is genuinely useful, and readers then go use the tool.

chunks.heading: Attention as well as time: why he built a scheduler
chunks.text:
- Curiosity Quench's mission was to help people stop scrolling. To promote it, he had to scroll while manually posting videos, and "you get sucked into the loop every time you manually post."
- So Post Bridge saves attention as well as time. He can post videos without opening Instagram and TikTok, which he calls "dreadful suck you in apps." He does not open them for months at a time.
- On the objection that he adds to the noise, he says he does not see a way to avoid that short of "not existing on the Internet."
- He does not moderate content. He leans on the official platform APIs, which moderate content themselves.
- He says he does not prevent abuse. He expects algorithms to push content people enjoy, and he hopes people make their own decisions about what to watch and post.

chunks.heading: Keeping the product lean as a solo founder
chunks.text:
- Jack mostly builds for what he uses day to day: "How can this make my day simpler and easier?"
- He adds a requested feature only if it is "very reasonable" and does not add a "super complex" workflow.
- For each change he asks whether it will bloat the software and make it less valuable to a normal first-time user.
- His rule: "if it still can remain simple, I'll add the feature." He wants to center the product on being as simple as possible.
- The next focus is content generation. He frames it as its own product that does not complicate the base tool; it only adds optionality.
- He does not use AI inside Post Bridge, which keeps it "bare bones as possible."

chunks.heading: Guided content generation instead of done-for-you AI
chunks.text:
- For visual content (video and images), his plan is aimed at businesses driving organic growth.
