- The vision has several parts:
  - Templates that have worked and produced results.
  - Instructions on how to use them.
  - Guidance on evoking a reaction or emotion from the target audience.
  - Ideas for each niche, since niches differ.
- Goal: guide someone to a valuable result, such as getting users to their product.
- He sizes the scope carefully: "if I go too narrow or go too wide, no one knows where to start." People do not know where to start, so he wants to provide a starting point. It is a "guided approach," not done for you completely.
- On shelf life, formats vary by platform, so he is always iterating. A format may work for five months or a year. He says people usually switch it out before results stop, because it feels repetitive. His rule: "if you have something that works, you keep using it," and when it stops working, iterate until you find something that works again.
- The content-generation aim is to help people find what is current. He admits that is hard because things change quickly, and says he will try rather than promise perfection.

chunks.heading: Social media as a public journal: doing first, posting second
chunks.text:
- Jack uses Twitter "like a personal public journal." He posts raw, unfiltered thoughts, often triggered by something he sees while building.
- His expectation: half the time no one sees a post, and about a tenth of the time a normal thought turns out controversial or big.
- He argues that because so much content is not human, honest posts with visible flaws will stand out and build something valuable "in a place where there's a lot of junk."
- He never aimed to grow Twitter. His goal was to make a valuable business and document it. The loop is "I post, I do something, I post, I do something," and it grows the business. Followers are a byproduct.
- He says the common opposite approach (grow followers to grow a business) does not work well, because people can tell when someone is really doing something versus "tweeting aphorisms."
- He admits to sometimes doing things so he can post about them, and works to play the game in a way that also serves his mental health, since constant posting drains you.
- He uses no AI for tweets: "I just post what's on my mind."

chunks.heading: Staying kind and not polarizing
chunks.text:
- He says being kind is partly conscious and partly personality ("people pleaser"). He accepts that people will be mad whatever he says, but there is a nicer way to say things.
- He tries to keep his opinions objective and non-alienating.
- He wants to attract the right people. After about a year, his replies are mostly very nice.
- He has blocked maybe three people, mostly mutes, and has never blocked a topic or word. He says his feed is curated by focusing on what he wants to see more of.
- He cites a kind, positive founder who inspired him.

chunks.heading: Engagement and notifications
chunks.text:
- He checks Twitter daily and replies to people there. Other platforms he checks roughly once a week or once a month, if he remembers.
- He does not automate replies, because it would be robotic. He argues there is good in not managing everything: "people realize you're a human."
- He keeps social media notifications off for everything. His only push notifications are texts from a few people.
- His view is that you cannot get to everything on the Internet. He thinks the original point of the internet was doing things when you want, and he is "unflipping it."

chunks.heading: Learning to code with AI and security
chunks.text:
- He uses Cursor to code. Less than two years before this interview (June 2025) he did not know how to code beyond basic HTML and CSS.
- He calls AI "an amazing tool for just rapid pace learning and understanding because no one's judging you."
- Outside coding, he does not use AI in his workflow, including customer service and blog posts. His reasoning: "If it's not a thousand percent beneficial, I don't bother." He likes the human aspect and the mistakes, and says he is "skeptical still."
- He does not object to others using AI to help write.
- On security: early on he understood that security mattered and checked things. He says many skip checks and get away with it until they have users and get hacked.
- He was attacked twice in a few months, partly because he was a proponent of vibe coding. No user data was harmed, and the main cost was a bigger bill from his provider.
- He learned the basics of securing sites quickly. He says it is a cat and mouse game and nobody is 100% secure.
- His advice: with customer information, "you can prompt your way to making something decently secure," but you should consider security. A hack or leak can end a business overnight. You should be careful, not scared.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jack Friks dropped out of college to make money online, tried print-on-demand, affiliate blogs, 2000+ YouTube videos and crypto, then learned to code. Post Bridge now makes $35K USD MRR, doubling in six months after an eight-month plateau. Only the intro is visible; the rest of the article is paywalled.

chunks.heading: Jack's path to Post Bridge: six years of failed online income attempts
chunks.text:
- Jack dropped out of his last semester of college about six years before writing. He wanted to make money online and control his own schedule and work.
- He says he "would be a miserable employee" in a traditional job, and that this drove him to try other routes.
- He spent roughly three years trying to earn money online before he learned to code.
- He then spent about another year trying to grow his first app. The Indie Hackers intro says he thought he was a failure until a new idea gained traction.
- Post Bridge is the idea that worked. By the intro's count, the whole stretch took four years of struggling.

chunks.heading: What Jack tried before learning to code
chunks.text:
Jack lists these experiments as part of "trying everything":

- Print-on-demand T-shirt designs.
- Affiliate marketing blog posts.
- YouTube videos: more than 2,000 in under two years.
- Crypto: "I made money and lost it all."

After these he decided to learn to code and build his own apps. None of the pre-coding experiments is credited with the eventual result in the available text.

chunks.heading: Post Bridge: product and revenue
chunks.text:
- Post Bridge is a social media scheduling tool for small teams, with agent-friendly workflows.
- Jack launched it about one and a half years before the article.
- It generates $50k CAD in MRR, which he gives as $35K USD.
- Most of his focus currently goes into Post Bridge.

chunks.heading: Growth shape: plateau, then doubling
chunks.text:
- MRR plateaued for eight months.
- In the last six months, Jack doubled MRR after that plateau.
- Growth was not a smooth curve. The article's framing is years of struggle, then a product that took off, then a flat stretch, then a second jump.

chunks.heading: Limits of this source
chunks.text: The rest of the essay is behind an Indie Hackers signup wall, so only the intro is available. Reader comments mention pricing, validation, hosting and other topics. Those are the commenters' paraphrases, not Jack's words, so they are left out here.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Self-maintained profile tracing Jack Friks from print-on-demand and crypto failures to Curiosity Quench, Post Bridge and Lovelee. Shows a solo founder building tools for his own problems, validating cheaply with short video, marketing organically about an hour a day, and publishing a public ledger of failures.

chunks.heading: Post Bridge: origin, build and launch model
chunks.text:
- Jack built Post Bridge from his own need. Marketing Curiosity Quench took him about an hour a day, half of it posting the same video to each platform by hand. The existing schedulers cost "like 10 times more than I want to pay."
- He first mentioned "a tool that helps me post all of the videos I'm making to Instagram, TikTok, Twitter, and YouTube all at once" in a build log on 28 September 2024.
- He validated the idea with mockups on TikTok before writing code.
- He built it in about a month, starting in September 2024. It launched in October 2024 with a hard paywall and no free tier.
- It is built on Next.js and Supabase. Jack runs it alone and answers support himself each morning before other work.
- It publishes to ten platforms: Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, LinkedIn, Facebook, Pinterest, Threads, Bluesky and Google Business. It has per-platform caption overrides, a calendar and a bulk upload tool.
- Pricing is set by the number of connected accounts, not per channel. Existing customers are grandfathered through price changes.

chunks.heading: Post Bridge revenue trajectory and public transparency
chunks.text:
- Post Bridge reached US$7,000 MRR after four and a half months.
- In June 2025 he ran a filmed challenge to reach US$30,000 a month without working past dinner. He reported US$12,000 on day 15, US$16,416 on day 21 and US$17,163 on day 24. The day-24 post came alongside a Y Combinator rejection.
- Indie Hackers described an eight-month plateau. Revenue then doubled in the first half of 2026 to about US$35,000 (CA$50,000) a month, roughly eighteen months after launch.
- Post Bridge publishes revenue in real time through TrustMRR, which reads it from Stripe. As of 6 September 2026 it showed about US$40,500 over the trailing 30 days and 1,725 active subscriptions.
- In spring 2025 he declined a public US$1 million offer for the company. He said it was "probably worth about half of that." He says the publicity of refusing added over US$100,000 in annual recurring revenue within a month.
- He keeps a public, spreadsheet-backed ledger of every project since 2019. It marks each as success, "okay" or failure and computes a hit rate. As of September 2026 it lists more than twenty projects, most marked as failures.

chunks.heading: Positioning Post Bridge as a publishing layer for AI agents
chunks.text:
- From 2026 Jack positioned Post Bridge as a publishing layer for AI agents. It ships a REST API, an MCP server and the `postbridge-cli` command-line tool, which was published to npm in June 2026. Assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT can list accounts, schedule and delete posts, and read analytics.
- An agent-mode skill repository went up on GitHub in March 2026.
- Post Bridge is listed in Anthropic's Claude connector directory and as a plugin inside ChatGPT.
- The product tagline is "Post to 10 social platforms from one place or your AI agent."
- Alongside the ChatGPT listing, Post Bridge published step-by-step guides to posting from ChatGPT, Claude, Grokbot and Gemini.
- Days after the ChatGPT listing surfaced in early September 2026, Post Bridge set four consecutive all-time daily signup records:
  - 4 September: 341
  - 5 September: 508
  - 6 September: 645
  - 7 September: 713
- The prior average was about 50 signups a day. Jack identified ChatGPT as the source.
- On the 5 September record day he reported 64 trials and 71 new customers.

chunks.heading: Organic short-form video marketing system
chunks.text:
- His marketing is entirely organic and takes about one hour a day.
- He builds short videos from formats that have already worked. He re-posts them until they stop working.
- He has a repeatable "2x2" template that he posted more than 300 times. He credits it with 60,000 to 70,000 signups.
- Starter Story reported in 2025 that his short-form videos had passed 300 million views.
- Curiosity Quench grew from six-second Instagram and TikTok videos about hobbies, several of which passed a million views.
- In the 30 days after September 2024, Curiosity Quench drew about 15 million views, 40,000 installs and US$12,000 in revenue.
- For Lovelee, a quote-tweet of the launch post brought 40,000 downloads in a week and a half. A TikTok and Instagram format he found added 11,000 downloads in 48 hours.
- A 31 October 2025 X post showing Lovelee as a shared grocery list reached 14.3 million views.
- On audiences, he says: "to not grow a personal brand at all. It's just to build cool things, do cool things, and then like share them."
- Each app gets its own Instagram and TikTok accounts. He built Lovelee as "my own case study" for Post Bridge.

chunks.heading: Curiosity Quench: validating, building and pricing the first app
chunks.text:
- Jack began Curiosity Quench in October 2023. It aims to reduce phone scrolling by giving users action plans for hobbies, with curated content for each step.
- He had tried and abandoned learning to code three or four times. It only stuck once he was building something he wanted to exist.
- He validated the idea with a 60-second TikTok that drew comments asking for the product.
- He built the first version in about four months while learning. He describes the process as feeding error messages into ChatGPT until it worked.
- He posted a numbered daily build log on YouTube for over a year.
- The app ran first on the web and reached the App Store in early 2024. It launched on Product Hunt on 28 April 2024 (day 196 of the log), after which he shut down the web version.
- It was priced at about US$30 a year with a seven-day trial.
- Downloads: 26,000 in a month by September 2024, and 100,000 total on 27 October 2024.
- Revenue: about US$3,000 a month by March 2025, and about US$60,000 in its first year. It later fell as he stopped marketing it.
- After the app appeared to peak at US$3,000 a month, a US$15,000 month came two months later.
- In December 2024, one year after he began coding, he reported over US$50,000 net income and US$7,000 MRR across his apps.

chunks.heading: Lovelee: a five-day launch challenge
chunks.text:
- Lovelee lets couples send hand-drawn notes to a partner's home screen. Jack built it for himself and his fiancée.
- He launched it in five days as part of a filmed two-month challenge to reach US$10,000 a month.
- At week six it had 56,000 downloads and US$3,194 MRR. His ledger records more than 100,000 downloads and about US$40,000 in revenue in the first six weeks.
- The launch tweet was "picked up by Russian news."

chunks.heading: Idea validation and solo operating principles
chunks.text:
- His core rule: the "easiest way to make a successful business is really just to solve your own problems."
- Before building, he asks whether he would pay to solve the problem.
- He tests demand with a landing page or short video: "if they don't click buy and a thousand people come, clearly the idea is probably not that good."
- He treats failure as normal and publishes it. His ledger includes abandoned apps and two books that sold poorly: the first at under 100 copies ("80% being family"), the second at about 20.
- He works alone in sprints rather than fixed hours. That runs from one or two hours a day in quiet periods to ten around a launch.
- He focuses on one project per day beyond customer support and stops at dinner time.
- Four years of earlier failures funded what came after:
  - Print-on-demand t-shirts and YouTube channels.
  - A Cardano crypto channel with 3.5 million views.
  - An NFT collection of 6,969 pieces. It sold out in a week, but most of the US$400,000 to 500,000 gross went to the developer's 40 percent commission, taxes and the market decline. That left about US$30,000 to 50,000 in profit.
- He keeps a folder of images captioned "keep going" that became a merchandise line.
